# **Be Born**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nací en Bogotá en 1990. | I was born in Bogotá in 1990. |

Spanish uses active **nacer**; English uses passive-form **be born**.

# **Be Worth**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El cuadro vale mucho y vale la pena protegerlo. | The painting is worth a lot, and it's worth protecting. |

Use **be worth + amount/noun/verb-ing**, not *worth to protect*.

# **Be Left** and **Be Missing**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quedan dos documentos, pero todavía falta una firma. | Two documents are left, but one signature is still missing. |

**Be left** means remain; **be missing** means be absent when expected.

# **Be Out Of**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nos quedamos sin café y casi no tenemos tiempo. | We're out of coffee and almost out of time. |

**Be out of something** means have none remaining.

# **Be About To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estoy a punto de salir; llámeme después. | I'm about to leave; call me later. |

**Be about to + base verb** describes the immediate future.

# **Be Used To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estoy acostumbrada a trabajar de noche. | I'm used to working at night. |

Here **to** is a preposition, so a following action uses **-ing**.

# **Be Interested In** and **Be Into**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A Ana le interesa la fotografía y le encanta la fotografía callejera. | Ana is interested in photography and is really into street photography. |

**Be interested in** is neutral; informal **be into** often suggests stronger enthusiasm.

# **Be Good At**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ana es buena para explicar ideas difíciles. | Ana is good at explaining difficult ideas. |

Use **be good at + noun/verb-ing** for skill.

# **Be Up To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los niños están muy callados; seguro traman algo. | The children are very quiet; they must be up to something. |

**Be up to something** often suggests a secret or suspicious activity. **It's up to you** instead assigns responsibility.

# **Be Right, Be Wrong**, and **Be at Fault**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tienes razón, yo estoy equivocado y el error fue culpa mía. | You're right, I'm wrong, and the error was my fault. |

Spanish uses **tener razón** and **equivocarse**; English uses **be right/wrong**. For responsibility, use **be someone's fault** or **be at fault**.

# **Be in a Hurry / Rush**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo afán, pero no quiero tomar una decisión apresurada. | I'm in a hurry, but I don't want to make a rushed decision. |

**Be in a hurry** and **be in a rush** translate Colombian Spanish **tener afán**.

# **Be Confident** and **Be Successful**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ana tiene confianza y ha tenido mucho éxito en su carrera. | Ana is confident and has been very successful in her career. |

Spanish often uses nouns with **tener**; English commonly uses the related adjectives with **be**.

# **Be About** a Topic

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La lección trata sobre los usos avanzados de **be**. | The lesson is about advanced uses of **be**. |

**Be about + topic** means concern or discuss that topic. Compare **be about to + verb**, which marks the immediate future.

# **Be Going To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Voy a llamar a Ana porque va a llover. | I'm going to call Ana because it's going to rain. |

**Be going to + verb** expresses a plan or evidence-based prediction; Spanish commonly uses **ir a + infinitive**.

# **Be Able To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quiero poder ayudar y mañana podré hacerlo. | I want to be able to help, and tomorrow I'll be able to. |

**Be able to** supplies infinitive, future, and perfect forms that **can** cannot build.

# Passive **Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me golpearon y el carro fue reparado ayer. | I was hit, and the car was repaired yesterday. |

**Be + past participle** can form the passive, shifting attention to the receiver of an action.

# Progressive **Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estoy trabajando y mañana estaré trabajando a esta hora. | I'm working, and tomorrow I'll be working at this time. |

**Be + verb-ing** builds progressive forms.

# Subjunctive **Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Es importante que estés aquí a tiempo. | It's important that you be here on time. |

Formal English can use unchanged **be** after demands, recommendations, or importance: **They requested that she be present**.

# **If I Were**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Si yo fuera usted, no lo haría; si fuera a hacerlo, llamaría primero. | If I were you, I wouldn't do it; if I were going to do it, I'd call first. |

Use **were** for formal or careful hypothetical meaning with every person. Informal **if I was** occurs, but **if I were you** is the standard fixed form.

# Perfect and Modal Forms of **Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ana ha estado aquí, podría estar cansada y debería estar en casa antes de las ocho. | Ana has been here, could be tired, and should be home before eight. |

Use **have/has been** for perfect forms and bare **be** after modals: **will, would, could, should, may**, or **might be**.

# **To Be**: **Be Going To** Use **be going to + base verb** for a future plan or a prediction based on present evidence. Spanish uses **ir a + infinitive** for the corresponding construction. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | voy a hacer algo | **I am going to do something** | | va a hacer algo | **he/she is going to do something** | | vas, vamos, van a hacer algo | **you/we/they are going to do something** | ## Future plan **Voy a estudiar inglés esta noche.**
I am going to study English tonight. The contraction is natural in speech: **I'm going to study English tonight.** Keep **to** before the action: **She is going to study.**
Not: *She is going study.*

# **To Be**: Present Forms and Contractions The present forms of **be** are **am**, **is**, and **are**. | Subject | Full form | Contraction | |---|---|---| | I | **I am** | **I'm** | | you | **you are** | **you're** | | he | **he is** | **he's** | | she | **she is** | **she's** | | it | **it is** | **it's** | | we | **we are** | **we're** | | they | **they are** | **they're** | The contraction has the same meaning as the full form: **Estoy listo.**
I am ready.
I'm ready. Use contractions naturally in conversation and informal writing. Use full forms when formality or emphasis makes them more appropriate.

# **To Be**: **Be Able To** and **Can** Use **be able to** or **can** to express ability. ## **Be able to** The form of **be** changes with the subject. Keep **to** before the action. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | poder hacer algo | **to be able to do something** | | puedo hacer algo | **I am able to do something** | | puede hacer algo | **he/she is able to do something** | | puedes, podemos, pueden hacer algo | **you/we/they are able to do something** | **Puedo explicar la actividad en inglés.**
I am able to explain the activity in English. ## **Can** **Can** does not change with the subject, and the next verb does not use **to**. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | poder hacer algo | **can do something** | **Puedo explicar la actividad en inglés.**
I can explain the activity in English. Compare the patterns: **I am able to do it.**
**I can do it.**
Not: *I can to do it.*

# Present and Past **There Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay un problema, hay dos opciones y ayer hubo tres errores. | There is a problem, there are two options, and there were three errors yesterday. |

Use **there + be** to introduce existence, translating impersonal Spanish **haber**.

# Future and Conditional **There Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Habrá una reunión; sin el cambio, habría más problemas. | There will be a meeting; without the change, there would be more problems. |

Change the form after **there**: **will be** for future and **would be** for conditional meaning.

# Modal **There Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Podría haber un error y debería haber una solución. | There could be an error, and there should be a solution. |

After a modal, use bare **be**: **there may/might/could/should be**.

# **There Is Going To Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Va a haber una reunión mañana y va a haber cambios. | There's going to be a meeting tomorrow, and there are going to be changes. |

# Perfect **There Be**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ha habido un error y ha habido varias quejas. | There has been an error, and there have been several complaints. |

Use **there has been** before singular and **there have been** before plural nouns.

# **To Be**: **There Is** and **There Are** Use **there is** or **there are** to say that something exists or is present. Spanish uses **hay** for both singular and plural nouns. English changes the form to agree with the noun. ## Singular | Spanish | English | |---|---| | hay + singular | **there is + singular** | **Hay un libro sobre la mesa.**
There is a book on the table. ## Plural | Spanish | English | |---|---| | hay + plural | **there are + plural** | **Hay tres libros sobre la mesa.**
There are three books on the table. In speech, **there is** commonly contracts to **there's**: **There's a book on the table.**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| She became angry. | Se puso brava. |

Spanish chooses the change verb according to the kind of result: **ponerse, volverse, hacerse, convertirse en**, or **llegar a ser**.

# **But** Meaning However

Use **but** to connect two contrasting ideas.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quería acompañarlos, pero no pude salir de la oficina a tiempo. | I wanted to join you, but I couldn't leave the office in time. |

The second idea conflicts with the speaker's intention. **Couldn't** is the standard contraction of **could not**.

# **But** Meaning Except

Before a noun or pronoun, **but** can mean **excepto**, **salvo** or **menos**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Todos entregaron el informe a tiempo menos Andrés, que lo envió al día siguiente. | Everyone but Andrés submitted the report on time; he sent his the next day. |

Here **but Andrés** excludes Andrés from **everyone**. It does not connect two contrasting clauses.

# **Not X but Y**

Use **not X but Y** to reject one description and replace it with the correct one. Spanish normally uses **no... sino...**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El problema no es el precio, sino el tiempo que tardará la entrega. | The problem isn't the price but the time the delivery will take. |

**But rather** can emphasize the correction: **The problem isn't the price but rather the delivery time.** The shorter **not X but Y** structure is usually sufficient.

# Spanish **Sino** Versus **Si No**

Spanish **sino** corrects or replaces an idea and becomes **but** or **but rather**. The two-word expression **si no** introduces a negative condition and becomes **if not**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No llamaremos hoy, sino mañana. | We won't call today but tomorrow. |
| Si no llamamos hoy, perderemos la reserva. | If we don't call today, we'll lose the reservation. |

When it states the consequence of not acting, English **otherwise** can also translate **si no**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenemos que llamar hoy; si no, perderemos la reserva. | We have to call today; otherwise, we'll lose the reservation. |

# **By** Meaning Beside

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Deje la caja junto a la puerta. | Leave the box by the door. |

For position, **by** means **beside, next to**, or **near**, depending on how precise the context is.

# Passing **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Pasé por la casa de Ana, pero no entré. | I went by Ana's house, but I didn't go in. |

With movement, **by** means past a place without necessarily stopping or entering.

# Deadline **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Debemos entregar el informe a más tardar el viernes a las doce. | We have to submit the report by twelve on Friday. |

**By** gives the latest acceptable time. The action may happen earlier.

# Creator or Agent: **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El informe fue escrito por Ana y aprobado por el gerente. | The report was written by Ana and approved by the manager. |

In a passive construction, **by** identifies who or what performs the action. It also names a creator: **a novel by García Márquez**.

# Transport: **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llegamos en carro, pero regresamos en bus. | We got there by car, but came back by bus. |

Use **by + transport** with no article: **by car, by bus, by plane**. Compare **in the car** and **on the bus** when referring to a particular vehicle.

# Method: **By + Verb-ing**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Mejoró su inglés practicando todos los días. | She improved her English by practicing every day. |

**By + verb-ing** explains the method used to obtain a result.

# Communication: **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Envíeme la confirmación por correo electrónico o por mensaje de texto. | Send me the confirmation by email or by text message. |

Use **by** to name a communication channel: **by email, by phone, by text**, or **by mail**.

# Rate, Unit, and Amount

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Les pagan por hora y los precios subieron un diez por ciento. | They're paid by the hour, and prices went up by ten percent. |

**By** can mark a unit or the amount of a change: **by the kilo, by ten points, little by little**.

# **Nearby**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay una farmacia cerca, pero no hay bancos cercanos. | There's a pharmacy nearby, but there are no nearby banks. |

**Nearby** is one word as an adverb or adjective. Standard English does not normally use *closeby*; use **close by** as two words.

# Fixed Expressions with **By**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Por cierto, ¿por casualidad viste a Ana? | By the way, did you see Ana by any chance? |

Learn **by the way** and **by any chance** as whole expressions; their meanings are not built from physical position.

# **By**: Beside and Past

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esperé junto a la ventana mientras Ana pasaba. | I waited by the window while Ana walked by. |

**By** can mark a position beside a reference point or movement past that point.

# **By** vs **Until**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Termine antes de las cinco; puede trabajar hasta las cinco. | Finish by five; you can work until five. |

**By five** sets the latest completion time. **Until five** says an activity continues up to that time.

# **By** vs **Through** for Means

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Mejoró practicando y consiguió el empleo por medio de un contacto. | She improved by practicing and got the job through a contact. |

**By + action** commonly names the method. **Through + noun** often names a process, channel, intermediary, or experience.

# **By, Near**, and **Next To**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Vivo cerca del parque, y mi edificio queda justo al lado de la biblioteca. | I live near the park, and my building is right next to the library. |

**Near** allows some distance. **Next to** means immediately beside. **By** means beside or close to without always specifying the exact distance.

# Passive **By** vs Instrument **With**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La ventana fue rota por Carlos con una piedra. | The window was broken by Carlos with a rock. |

**By** identifies the agent who performed the action. **With** identifies the tool or instrument used.

# **Call → Llamar** by Phone

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Call Ana when you arrive. | Llama a Ana cuando llegues. |

For telephone contact, **call someone** becomes **llamar a alguien**. Spanish requires personal **a**.

# **Be Called → Llamarse**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| This dish is called a tamal, and the restaurant is called El Patio. | Este plato se llama tamal y el restaurante se llama El Patio. |

For names, English passive **be called** commonly becomes Spanish pronominal **llamarse**.

# **Call → Llamar / Mandar Llamar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Call the doctor immediately. | Llama al médico de inmediato. |

For summoning someone, use **llamar** or **mandar llamar**.

# **Call → Llamar / Considerar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I call that a serious mistake. | Yo considero que eso es un error grave. |

When assigning a description, Spanish may use **llamar, considerar**, or a clause with **decir**.

# **Call Off → Cancelar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| They called off the meeting. | Cancelaron la reunión. |

**Call off** means cancel an event, search, or action: **cancelar** or **suspender**.

# **Call On → Pedir / Visitar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The teacher called on me to answer. | La profesora me pidió que respondiera. |

**Call on** can select someone to speak, request action, or visit someone formally.

# **Call For → Requerir / Exigir**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| This situation calls for patience. | Esta situación requiere paciencia. |

**Call for** can mean require, demand, or publicly request.

# **Call Back → Devolver La Llamada**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I'll call you back after lunch. | Te devuelvo la llamada después del almuerzo. |

For returning a phone call, use **devolver la llamada** or **volver a llamar**.

# Communication Verbs: Calling Somebody Use **call + somebody**. Do not put **to** before the person. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | llamar a alguien | **to call somebody** | **Llamo a mi mamá después del trabajo.**
I call my mother after work. **Call Laura.**
Not: *Call to Laura.*

# **To Be**: **Be Able To** and **Can** Use **be able to** or **can** to express ability. ## **Be able to** The form of **be** changes with the subject. Keep **to** before the action. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | poder hacer algo | **to be able to do something** | | puedo hacer algo | **I am able to do something** | | puede hacer algo | **he/she is able to do something** | | puedes, podemos, pueden hacer algo | **you/we/they are able to do something** | **Puedo explicar la actividad en inglés.**
I am able to explain the activity in English. ## **Can** **Can** does not change with the subject, and the next verb does not use **to**. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | poder hacer algo | **can do something** | **Puedo explicar la actividad en inglés.**
I can explain the activity in English. Compare the patterns: **I am able to do it.**
**I can do it.**
Not: *I can to do it.*

# **Can** for a Learned Skill

For learned abilities such as swimming, reading, or driving, Spanish often uses **saber + infinitive** rather than **poder**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Sé nadar. | I can swim. |
| No sabe manejar. | She can't drive. |

# Uses of **Can**

English **can** maps to **poder** for ability or permission and often to **saber + infinitive** for a learned skill.

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [Can and Be Able To](01-can-and-be-able-to.md) | Puedo hacerlo. | I can do it. |
| [Learned Skill](02-can-for-a-learned-skill.md) | Sé nadar. | I can swim. |

See Spanish **poder** in the PostgreSQL curriculum database for ability, permission, possibility, and requests.

# **Close Down**

Use **close down** when a business or operation stops functioning. Spanish commonly uses **cerrar** or **clausurar**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Cerraron la fábrica el año pasado. | They closed down the factory last year. |
| Las autoridades clausuraron el local. | The authorities closed down the establishment. |

# **Closing**

English **closing** can become **cierre**, **clausura**, or the act of finalizing an agreement.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| el cierre de la tienda | the store closing |
| la clausura del evento | the closing of the event |
| el cierre del trato | the closing of the deal |

# English **Could**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| When I was young, I could run fast. | Cuando era joven, podía correr rápido. |
| I managed to open the door yesterday. | Ayer pude abrir la puerta. |
| It could rain later. | Podría llover más tarde. |
| Could you help me? | ¿Podrías ayudarme? |
| She could have called. | Podría haber llamado. |

Past ability, successful completion, possibility, politeness, and unreal past possibility do not all use the same Spanish form.

# English **Cover**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Cover the food. | Tapa la comida. |
| The course covers five topics. | El curso abarca cinco temas. |
| Insurance covers the damage. | El seguro cubre los daños. |
| Can you cover my shift? | ¿Puedes reemplazarme en mi turno? |
| We covered twenty kilometers. | Recorrimos veinte kilómetros. |

Physical covering, including a scope, paying a cost, substituting for someone, and traveling a distance require different Spanish choices.

# English **Cut**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Cut the paper. | Corta el papel. |
| They cut the budget. | Redujeron el presupuesto. |
| The storm cut the power. | La tormenta interrumpió la electricidad. |
| Cut the sentence from the report. | Elimina la oración del informe. |
| The road cuts through the forest. | La carretera atraviesa el bosque. |

Physical cutting, reduction, interruption, deletion, and crossing a space require different Spanish choices.

# **Deal → Repartir** Cards

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Deal five cards to each player. | Reparte cinco cartas a cada jugador. |

For distributing playing cards, **deal** becomes **repartir**.

# **Deal → Acuerdo / Trato**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| We made a deal yesterday. | Hicimos un acuerdo ayer. |

For an agreement, **deal** becomes **acuerdo, trato**, or **negocio**, depending on formality and context.

# **A Good Deal → Una Buena Oferta / Un Buen Negocio**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| That laptop was a good deal. | Ese portátil estaba a muy buen precio. |

For favorable value, use **buena oferta, buen precio**, or **buen negocio**.

# **A Great Deal → Mucho / Gran Cantidad**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The repair requires a great deal of time. | La reparación requiere mucho tiempo. |

Quantity **a great deal of** becomes **mucho/mucha** or **una gran cantidad de**.

# **Deal With → Manejar / Resolver**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| We need to deal with this problem today. | Tenemos que resolver este problema hoy. |

For handling a situation, use **manejar, resolver, abordar**, or **lidiar con**.

# **Deal With → Tratar Con**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I deal with customers every day. | Trato con clientes todos los días. |

For interacting or doing business with people, **deal with** becomes **tratar con, atender**, or **trabajar con**.

# **Deal In → Comerciar Con / Dedicarse A**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The company deals in medical equipment. | La empresa comercializa equipos médicos. |

For buying and selling a category of goods, use **comercializar, comerciar con**, or **dedicarse a**.

# **No Big Deal → No Es Gran Cosa**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| It's no big deal; we can fix it. | No es gran cosa; podemos arreglarlo. |

This informal expression becomes **no es gran cosa, no pasa nada**, or **no es para tanto**, depending on tone.

Produce promised outcome.

# English **Do**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I do my homework after dinner. | Hago la tarea después de cenar. |
| Laura does the dishes. | Laura lava los platos. |
| Mateo is doing well at work. | A Mateo le está yendo bien en el trabajo. |
| Diana did her hair before the interview. | Diana se arregló el pelo antes de la entrevista. |
| Do you work here? | ¿Trabajas aquí? |

Lexical **do** often becomes **hacer**, but natural combinations may require another verb. Auxiliary **do** normally has no separate Spanish word.

# **Any** Versus **Either**

**Either** normally chooses between two; **any** allows a choice from a larger or unrestricted group.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Puedes escoger cualquiera de los dos libros o cualquier libro de toda la biblioteca. | You can choose either book or any book in the entire library. |

# **Both, Either**, and **Neither**

**Both** includes the two, **either** selects one of the two, and **neither** rejects the two.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ambos libros son buenos, cualquiera sirve y ninguno está en la biblioteca. | Both books are good, either one works, and neither one is in the library. |

# **Either Of**

Use **either of + two known choices**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Cualquiera de los dos libros sirve para la clase. | Either of the two books works for the class. |

A singular verb is clearest in careful English.

# **Either One**

**Either one** means either of two known choices is acceptable.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —¿Cuál quieres? —Cualquiera de los dos. | “Which one do you want?” “Either one.” |

# **Either...Or**

Use **either A or B** when one of two options applies.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Podemos reunirnos o el lunes o el martes. | We can meet either Monday or Tuesday. |

# **Either Way**

**Either way** means whichever of the two possibilities happens.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Podemos ir en bus o caminar; de cualquier manera, llegaremos antes de las ocho. | We can take the bus or walk; either way, we'll arrive before eight. |

# **Not...Either**

At the end of a negative statement, **either** means **tampoco**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Laura no va a asistir y Carlos tampoco va a ir. | Laura isn't going to attend, and Carlos isn't going either. |

# Pronunciation: **Either** and **Neither**

Both words have two standard first vowels: `/ˈiːðər/` or `/ˈaɪðər/`, and `/ˈniːðər/` or `/ˈnaɪðər/`.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Cualquiera de las dos pronunciaciones sirve; ninguna es incorrecta. | Either pronunciation works; neither one is wrong. |

Speakers may use either variant regardless of country.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|

# **Where, When**, and **How Else?**

Place **else** after a question word to ask for another place, time, or method.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Dónde más podríamos reunirnos y de qué otra manera llegaríamos? | Where else could we meet, and how else would we get there? |

# **Something Else**

**Something else** means another unidentified thing.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esto no funciona; intentemos algo más. | This isn't working; let's try something else. |

Informally, **That was something else!** can mean extraordinary.

# **Anything Else**

Use **anything else** in neutral questions and negatives.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Necesitas algo más? No puedo comprar nada más hoy. | Do you need anything else? I can't buy anything else today. |

# **Nothing Else**

**Nothing else** means no other thing.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No quiero nada más; con esto basta. | I don't want anything else; I need nothing else. |

The paired sentence contrasts **not...anything else** with **nothing else**.

# **Everything Else**

**Everything else** means all the other things.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El precio está bien, pero todo lo demás tiene que cambiar. | The price is fine, but everything else has to change. |

# **Someone Else** and **Somebody Else**

Both expressions mean another unidentified person.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Pídele a alguien más que revise las cifras. | Ask someone else to check the figures. |

Use these forms in neutral questions and negatives.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Hay alguien más aquí? No vi a nadie más al entrar. | Is anyone else here? I didn't see anybody else when I came in. |

# **No One Else** and **Nobody Else**

Both expressions mean no other person and contain their own negative idea.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nadie más tiene acceso al archivo. | No one else has access to the file. |

# **Everyone Else** and **Everybody Else**

Both expressions mean all the other people.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Todos los demás ya terminaron, pero yo apenas empecé. | Everyone else has already finished, but I've only just started. |

# **Someone Else's**

Add **'s** after **else** to show that something belongs to another person.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tomé el paraguas de otra persona por accidente. | I took someone else's umbrella by accident. |

Write **someone else's**, not *someone's else*.

# **Or Else**

**Or else** introduces a consequence or threat if the instruction isn't followed.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenemos que salir ya o, si no, perderemos el bus. | We've gotta leave now, or else we'll miss the bus. |

Without a stated result, **Or else!** sounds threatening.

# **Elsewhere**

**Elsewhere** means in or to another place.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aquí no tienen el repuesto, así que tendremos que buscarlo en otra parte. | They don't have the part here, so we'll have to look elsewhere. |

# Pronunciation: **Else** and **Elves**

**Else** ends in `/ls/`; **elves** adds a `/v/`. They aren't homophones.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Qué más podrían esconder los elfos en otra parte? | What else could the elves hide elsewhere? |

The playful sentence repeats **else / elves / elsewhere**.

# **Even** for Surprising Inclusion

Use **even** to include someone or something that the listener would not expect.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Todos resolvieron el problema; incluso Laura, que no había asistido a la clase, dio la respuesta correcta. | Everyone solved the problem; even Laura, who had not attended the class, gave the correct answer. |

The surprise is that Laura succeeded despite missing the class.

# **Even If**

Use **even if** when a possible condition will not change the result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Incluso si llueve mañana, jugaremos el partido porque el estadio tiene techo. | Even if it rains tomorrow, we will play the game because the stadium has a roof. |

The rain is only a possibility, and the roof guarantees that it will not change the plan.

# **Even Though**

Use **even though** when a fact is real but contrasts strongly with the result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque llovió toda la mañana, jugamos el partido porque el estadio tenía techo. | Even though it rained all morning, we played the game because the stadium had a roof. |

Unlike **even if**, this sentence confirms that the rain really happened.

# **Even When**

Use **even when** when the same result continues in a particular or repeated situation.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Andrés va al trabajo en bicicleta todos los días, incluso cuando llueve. | Andrés rides his bicycle to work every day, even when it rains. |

**Every day** makes it clear that rainy days are included in a repeated habit.

# **Not Even**

Use **not even** when someone or something fails to reach an expected minimum.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Laura estaba tan enojada que se fue sin despedirse y ni siquiera cerró la puerta. | Laura was so angry that she left without saying goodbye and did not even close the door. |

Closing the door is presented as the minimum expected action.

# **Even** Before a Comparison

Before a comparative, **even** increases the degree of the comparison.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El segundo examen fue aún más difícil que el primero, aunque tuvimos una hora adicional para terminarlo. | The second exam was even more difficult than the first, although we had an extra hour to finish it. |

Here **even** intensifies **more difficult**; it does not mean **incluso**.

# **Even So**

Use **even so** to show that a fact did not prevent a contrasting result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El plazo era de solo dos días; aun así, entregamos el proyecto completo y a tiempo. | The deadline was only two days; even so, we delivered the complete project on time. |

**Even so** refers back to the short deadline and introduces the unexpected result.

# **Even As**

Use **even as** to emphasize that two things happen at exactly the same time, often with a surprising contrast.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Justo cuando el director anunciaba los recortes, la empresa reportó ganancias récord. | Even as the director announced the cuts, the company reported record profits. |

The two simultaneous events create the contrast. Depending on context, **even as** can be **justo cuando**, **al mismo tiempo que** or **incluso mientras**.

# **Even Now** and **Even Then**

Before a time expression, **even** emphasizes that something remains surprising at that time.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Han pasado veinte años desde el accidente y, aún ahora, Marta evita conducir de noche. | Twenty years have passed since the accident, and even now, Marta avoids driving at night. |

The twenty-year interval makes Marta's continuing reaction surprising. The same pattern gives **even then → aun entonces / incluso en ese momento**.

# **Even** and **Odd** Numbers

An **even number** is divisible by two; an **odd number** is not.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Doce es un número par porque se puede dividir exactamente entre dos, pero trece es impar. | Twelve is an even number because it can be divided exactly by two, but thirteen is odd. |

Learn the contrast together: **even and odd → par e impar**.

# **Even** Meaning Level

As an adjective, **even** can describe a surface without slopes or irregularities.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La mesa se tambalea porque el piso no está nivelado. | The table wobbles because the floor is not even. |

The wobbling shows that **even** describes the physical level of the floor.

# **Even** Meaning Steady

**Even** can describe something that remains regular, constant, or calm instead of fluctuating.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque estaba nerviosa, Paula mantuvo una voz tranquila y constante durante toda la entrevista. | Although she was nervous, Paula maintained a calm, even voice throughout the interview. |

Her nervousness makes the steadiness of her voice significant. In other contexts, **an even pace** or **an even temperature** can mean **un ritmo constante** or **una temperatura estable**.

# **Even** Meaning Equally Distributed

**Even** can mean that an amount is divided or distributed equally.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dividimos las veinte tareas en partes iguales, así que cada miembro del equipo recibió cinco. | We made an even division of the twenty tasks, so each team member received five. |

The equal result identifies **even** as **igual**, **uniforme** or **equitativo**, not **nivelado**.

# **Even** Meaning Equal

**Even** can mean that neither side is ahead.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Cada equipo ha ganado dos partidos, así que están empatados antes de la final. | Each team has won two games, so they are even before the final. |

The equal number of victories establishes the meaning.

# **An Even Chance**

An **even chance** means that two possible outcomes are equally likely.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Según el médico, hay las mismas probabilidades de que el tratamiento funcione o no funcione. | According to the doctor, there is an even chance that the treatment will work or fail. |

The two equally probable outcomes establish the fifty-fifty meaning.

# **An Even Amount**

Before a round number or amount, **even** can mean **exactly**, with no fraction or remainder.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Después de pagar todos los cargos, la cuenta quedó en cien dólares exactos, sin centavos adicionales. | After all the fees were paid, the bill came to an even one hundred dollars, with no additional cents. |

Here **even** means **exactos** or **redondos**, not **pares**.

# **Even Out**

**Even out** means to reduce a difference and make something more balanced.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Trabajaremos menos horas el viernes para equilibrar la carga de trabajo después de tres días muy largos. | We will work fewer hours on Friday to even out the workload after three very long days. |

The shorter Friday compensates for the longer days.

# **Even the Score**

As a verb, **even** can make a score, record, or competition equal.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El equipo visitante perdía dos a uno, pero marcó en el último minuto para empatar el marcador. | The visiting team was losing two to one, but it scored in the final minute to even the score. |

The final goal changes unequal scores into equal scores.

# **Get Even**

**Get even with someone** means to retaliate for something that person did.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tomás dañó mi bicicleta a propósito, pero no voy a vengarme de él dañando la suya. | Tomás damaged my bicycle on purpose, but I am not going to get even with him by damaging his. |

The repeated act of damage makes the idea of retaliation explicit.

# **We Are Even**

**We are even** means that neither person owes the other anything.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tú pagaste la cena y yo pagué el taxi por el mismo valor, así que estamos a mano. | You paid for dinner and I paid the same amount for the taxi, so we are even. |

The equal payments settle the debt between the two people.

# **Break Even**

In business, **break even** means that income and costs are equal, so there is neither a profit nor a loss.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Producir el evento cuesta cinco millones de pesos, así que debemos recibir cinco millones por la venta de entradas para quedar en punto de equilibrio. | The event costs five million pesos to produce, so we must take in five million pesos from ticket sales to break even. |

The equal cost and income establish the break-even point.

# **Have You Ever...?**

Use **have/has + person + ever + past participle** to ask whether something has happened at any time in someone's life.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Alguna vez has viajado sola a otro país? | Have you ever traveled alone to another country? |

The exact time isn't important. If the question names a finished time, use the simple past: **Did you travel alone last year?**

# **If You Ever...**

Use **if + person + ever** for something that may happen at any future time.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Si alguna vez necesitas ayuda con el contrato, llámame. | If you ever need help with the contract, call me. |

English uses the present form after **if**, even when the possibility is in the future.

# **Don't Ever** and **Never**

Both forms can give a strong negative warning.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nunca vuelvas a compartir tu contraseña con nadie. | Don't ever share your password with anyone again. |

**Never share it again** has the same core message. **Don't ever** often sounds especially direct and emotional.

# **Almost Never** and **Hardly Ever**

Both expressions mean that something happens very rarely.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Casi nunca cocinamos entre semana porque llegamos tarde a casa. | We hardly ever cook during the week because we get home late. |

**Almost never** is equally clear. **Hardly ever** is extremely common in conversation.

# **The Best Ever**

Place **ever** after a superlative to compare something with every relevant time before now.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esta es la mejor clase que hemos tenido. | This is the best class we've ever had. |

Informal **the best class ever** expresses the same enthusiastic idea.

# **More Than Ever**

Use **more than ever** when something is stronger, greater, or more necessary now than at any previous time.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Después de perder los archivos, necesitamos copias de seguridad más que nunca. | After losing the files, we need backups more than ever. |

# **Ever Since**

Use **ever since + starting point** for a situation that began then and has continued until now.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Desde que tuve el accidente, siempre he tomado el bus. | I've taken the bus ever since I had the accident. |

The shorter **I've taken the bus since the accident** is often more natural when no extra emphasis is needed.

# **Forever**

**Forever** means for all future time or for a period that feels extremely long.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No podemos esperar eternamente; llevamos horas aquí. | We can't wait forever; we've been here for hours. |

The one-word spelling **forever** is standard. British English also uses **for ever**, especially for the literal meaning.

# **Happily Ever After**

In stories, **happily ever after** means happily for the rest of one's life.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El cuento termina diciendo que vivieron felices para siempre. | The story ends by saying that they lived happily ever after. |

Outside fairy tales, speakers often use the phrase playfully or skeptically.

# **Ever-Growing** and **Ever-Changing**

Before a description ending in **-ing**, **ever-** can mean continually.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenemos que adaptarnos a una lista de requisitos que crece y cambia constantemente. | We've gotta adapt to an ever-growing, ever-changing list of requirements. |

These compounds are more common in formal or polished writing than in relaxed conversation.

# **Whoever**

**Whoever** means any person who or no matter who.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quien haya dejado este paquete debe recogerlo antes de las cinco. | Whoever left this package has to pick it up before five. |

The complete **whoever** idea can be the subject of the sentence.

# **Whatever**

**Whatever** can mean anything that or no matter what.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Escoge lo que quieras; yo comeré lo mismo que tú. | Choose whatever you want; I'll have the same thing as you. |

Used alone as a response—**Whatever**—it can sound dismissive or rude.

# **Whenever**

**Whenever** can mean every time that or at any time that.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llámame cuando quieras; casi nunca apago el teléfono. | Call me whenever you want; I hardly ever turn my phone off. |

# **Wherever**

**Wherever** means anywhere that or no matter where.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dondequiera que trabajes, guarda siempre una copia de tus archivos. | Wherever you work, always keep a copy of your files. |

# **Whichever**

Use **whichever** when any option from a limited known group is acceptable.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Puedes tomar cualquiera de los dos buses; ambos paran frente al banco. | You can take whichever bus comes first; both stop in front of the bank. |

**Whatever** is broader; **whichever** points to a defined choice.

# Pronunciation: **Ever, Never**, and **Every**

**Ever** has two syllables, **never** adds `/n/`, and **every** normally has two syllables in natural speech. None has a common homophone.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Toda persona inteligente que he conocido nunca dice “nunca jamás”. | Every clever person I've ever met never says “never ever.” |

The playful repetition contrasts **every**, **ever**, **never**, and **clever** without treating them as homophones.

# **Everyone** and **Everybody**

Both words mean every person and take a singular verb.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Todos están listos, pero cada uno tiene que traer su propia identificación. | Everyone's ready, but everybody has to bring their own ID. |

# **Everything** and **Everywhere**

**Everything** covers all things; **everywhere** covers all places.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Buscamos por todas partes y revisamos todo, pero no encontramos la llave. | We looked everywhere and checked everything, but we didn't find the key. |

# **A Few, Few, A Little**, and **Little**

| Noun type | Positive amount | Insufficient amount |
|---|---|---|
| countable plural | a few cats | few cats |
| uncountable | a little time | little time |

The article **a** changes the practical meaning:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo unos cuantos libros. | I have a few books. |

**A few / a little** present the amount as available. **Few / little** emphasize that the amount is small or not enough.

# **Be** the State; **Get** the Change

Use **be + adjective** for a state and **get + adjective** for the transition into it.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Antes era pobre, luego me volví rico y ahora soy rico. | I was poor, then I got rich, and now I'm rich. |

The reusable timeline is **wasn't X → got X → am X**. **Get** doesn't replace every use of **be**; it replaces the moment of becoming.

# **Be Ready** and **Get Ready**

**Be ready** means estar listo. **Get ready** means alistarse or prepararse.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No estaba listo, así que me alisté y ahora estoy listo. | I wasn't ready, so I got ready, and now I'm ready. |

The natural instruction is **Get ready—we've gotta go!**

# **Be Busy** and **Get Busy**

**Be busy** describes being occupied. **Get busy** means become busy or start working actively.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La mañana estaba tranquila, luego me ocupé y ahora estoy muy ocupado. | My morning was quiet, then I got busy, and now I'm really busy. |

As an instruction, **Get busy!** means start working, not merely enter a busy state.

# **Be Tired** and **Get Tired**

**Be tired** describes tiredness. **Get tired** describes becoming tired.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenía mucha energía, pero me cansé y ahora estoy cansado. | I was full of energy, but I got tired, and now I'm tired. |

**I'm tired of waiting** means estoy cansado de esperar; **I'm getting tired of waiting** means that frustration is increasing.

# **Be Married** and **Get Married**

**Be married** describes marital status. **Get married** means casarse.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No estaban casados, se casaron en junio y ahora están casados. | They weren't married, they got married in June, and now they're married. |

Say **get married to someone**, not **get married with someone**.

# **Be Dark** and **Get Dark**

**Be dark** describes darkness. **Get dark** describes the light changing.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estaba soleado, luego oscureció y ahora está oscuro. | It was sunny, then it got dark, and now it's dark. |

The minimal change keeps the timeline clear: **It isn't dark, it's getting dark, and soon it'll be dark.**

# **Be Angry** and **Get Angry**

**Be angry** describes the emotion. **Get angry** means become angry or enojarse.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estaba tranquilo, pero me enojé y ahora estoy enojado. | I was calm, but I got angry, and now I'm angry. |

Use **angry with someone** and **angry about something**: **She got angry with me about the delay.**

# **Be Rich** and **Get Rich**

**Be rich** describes wealth. **Get rich** means become rich or enriquecerse.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Era pobre, se hizo rico lentamente y ahora es rico. | He was poor, he slowly got rich, and now he's rich. |

**Get rich quick** is a common fixed idea for becoming rich rapidly, often through a questionable plan.

# **Be Better** and **Get Better**

**Be better** describes an improved state. **Get better** describes improvement.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estaba enferma, se mejoró y ahora está mucho mejor. | She was sick, she got better, and now she's much better. |

**Get better** works for health, skills, situations, and conditions: **My English is getting better.**

# **Be Hungry** and **Get Hungry**

English uses **be hungry** for tener hambre and **get hungry** for empezar a tener hambre.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|

For a person's sensation, **be cold** means tener frío and **get cold** means empezar a tener frío.

|---|---|

# **Get Someone To Do** Versus **Have Someone Do**

Both patterns can mean arranging for another person to do something, but their forms are different.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Conseguí que Ana pintara la puerta y le pedí al técnico que arreglara la ventana. | I got Ana to paint the door, and I had the technician fix the window. |

- **get + person + to + verb** often suggests persuasion or effort: **I got Ana to help.**
- **have + person + verb** often suggests an arrangement, request, or instruction: **I had Ana help.**

Don't add **to** after the person with **have**: **I had him do it**, not **I had him to do it**.

# **Do It, Get It Done**, and **Have It Done**

Spanish may use **hazlo** for all three ideas, but English changes the focus.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¡Hazlo tú, asegúrate de que quede listo o encárgale el trabajo a alguien, pero tiene que estar listo hoy! | Do it, get it done, or have it done, but it's gotta be ready today! |

- **Do it!** — perform the action yourself.
- **Get it done!** — make sure it gets completed; you may do it or involve someone else.
- **Have it done!** — arrange or instruct someone else to do it.

The difference isn't always visible in **hazlo**, so the situation determines which English form fits.

# **Get** or **Have Something Finished, Sent**, or **Sold**

The result pattern is productive: **get/have + thing + completed form**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenemos que terminar el informe, enviar el paquete y vender el carro, así que hagamos que todo quede listo esta semana. | We've gotta get the report finished, get the package sent, and get the car sold this week. |

**Get** often emphasizes achieving the result, sometimes after effort. **Have** more clearly suggests arranging for someone else to produce it:

- **I'll get the package sent today.**
- **I'll have the package sent by my assistant.**

The playful rhythm—**get it finished, get it sent, get it sold**—helps fix the reusable frame.

# **Did It** Versus **Got It Done**

An active verb says the subject performed the action. **Get + thing + past participle** says the subject caused or arranged the result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ellos vendieron el carro directamente, pero consiguieron que un agente vendiera la casa. | They sold the car themselves, but they got the house sold by an agent. |

- **They sold it.** — they performed the sale.
- **They got it sold.** — they made sure it was sold; someone else may have performed the sale.
- **They got it done.** — they made sure the unspecified task was completed.

The reusable form is **get + thing + past participle**: **get it sold, get it sent, get it fixed**.

# **Make Sure I Do It** Versus **Make Sure It Gets Done**

Both promises guarantee completion, but only one identifies the person who will perform the action.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me aseguraré de hacerlo yo; si no puedo, me aseguraré de que quede listo de todos modos. | I'll make sure I do it; if I can't, I'll make sure it gets done anyway. |

- **I'll make sure I do it.** — I personally commit to doing it.
- **I'll make sure it gets done.** — I commit to the result; I or someone else may do it.

The **get** passive hides the actor and creates a useful ladder:

- **Somebody will do it.** — the actor is somebody.
- **It will get done.** — the task becomes the focus; the actor disappears.
- **I'll make sure it gets done.** — I take responsibility for ensuring that somebody, possibly me, does it.
- **I'll get it done.** — I cause or ensure the same completed result.

So **It will get done** can be taught as **Somebody will do it** with the person removed. It doesn't, by itself, say who will make sure.

# **Had Him Killed** Versus **Got Him Killed**

Both expressions connect one person's actions to another person's death, but they normally assign intention differently.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El jefe mandó a matar a Leo; el informante causó la muerte de Leo al revelar dónde estaba. | The boss had Leo killed; the informant got Leo killed by revealing his location. |

- **He had him killed.** — he deliberately ordered or arranged for someone to kill him.
- **He got him killed.** — something he did caused or led to the killing, often unintentionally.

The structure explains the difference:

- **have + person + killed** focuses on arranging the action.
- **get + person + killed** focuses on causing the resulting state or event.

Context can make **got him killed** deliberate, but it doesn't automatically mean that he gave the order. The same pattern appears without another person: **He got himself killed** means his own actions led to his death, not that he hired someone to kill him.

# Causative **Get**

Use causative **get** when someone causes, persuades, arranges, or ensures an action or result.

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [**Get Someone To Do Something**](01-get-someone-to-do-something.md) | Quiero que alguien arregle la puerta, así que conseguiré que mi hermano la arregle. | I want someone to fix the door, so I'll get my brother to fix it. |
| [**Get Someone To Do** Versus **Have Someone Do**](02-get-someone-to-do-versus-have-someone-do.md) | Conseguí que Ana pintara la puerta y le pedí al técnico que arreglara la ventana. | I got Ana to paint the door, and I had the technician fix the window. |
| [Person Versus Result](03-get-someone-to-do-it-versus-get-it-done.md) | Conseguiré que alguien arregle el informe y me aseguraré de que quede listo. | I'll get someone to fix the report, and I'll get it done. |
| [**Do It, Get It Done**, and **Have It Done**](04-do-it-get-it-done-and-have-it-done.md) | Hazlo tú, asegúrate de que quede listo o mándalo a hacer. | Do it, get it done, or have it done. |
| [Finished, Sent, or Sold](05-get-or-have-something-finished-sent-or-sold.md) | Tenemos que terminar el informe, enviar el paquete y vender el carro. | We've gotta get the report finished, the package sent, and the car sold. |
| [**Did It** Versus **Got It Done**](06-did-it-versus-got-it-done.md) | Ellos vendieron el carro, pero consiguieron que un agente vendiera la casa. | They sold the car, but they got the house sold by an agent. |
| [**Make Sure I Do It** Versus **It Gets Done**](07-make-sure-i-do-it-versus-it-gets-done.md) | Me aseguraré de hacerlo yo; si no puedo, me aseguraré de que quede listo de todos modos. | I'll make sure I do it; if I can't, I'll make sure it gets done anyway. |
| [**Had Him Killed** Versus **Got Him Killed**](08-had-him-killed-versus-got-him-killed.md) | El jefe mandó a matar a Leo; el informante causó la muerte de Leo al revelar dónde estaba. | The boss had Leo killed; the informant got Leo killed by revealing his location. |

## Mastery Phrases

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quiero que alguien lo haga, conseguiré que Ana lo haga y me aseguraré de que quede listo. | I want someone to do it, I'll get Ana to do it, and I'll get it done. |
| Yo lo arreglé, conseguí que Ana lo arreglara y mandé a arreglarlo. | I fixed it, I got Ana to fix it, and I had it fixed. |
| Me aseguraré de hacerlo yo; si no puedo, me aseguraré de que se haga y conseguiré que quede listo. | I'll make sure I do it; if I can't, I'll make sure it gets done and I'll get it done. |
| Alguien lo hará, así que se hará; yo me aseguraré de que se haga. | Somebody will do it, so it will get done; I'll make sure it gets done. |
| El jefe mandó a matarlo, pero el informante causó su muerte sin dar la orden. | The boss had him killed, but the informant got him killed without giving the order. |

# **Get It**: Understand

In conversation, **get** can mean understand an idea, explanation, joke, or situation.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Al principio no entendía el chiste, pero ahora sí lo entiendo. | I didn't get the joke at first, but now I get it. |

Context separates several common meanings:

- **I got it.** — I understood it or received it.
- **I've got it.** — I understand, possess it, or will handle it.
- **You got it.** — I understand your request and will do it.

The playful progression is **I didn't get it, then I got it, and now I've got it.**

# **Get Something To Someone** or Somewhere

**Get + thing + to + recipient/place** means make sure the thing reaches its destination.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Te enviaré el informe mañana y haré que los originales lleguen a la oficina antes del viernes. | I'll get the report to you tomorrow and get the originals to the office by Friday. |

**Send** names one method. **Get it to you** emphasizes successful delivery and may involve sending it, carrying it, or asking someone else to deliver it.

Keep the two meanings together: **I got it, and I'll get it to you tomorrow.**

# Everyday Replacements with **Get**

These uses replace a more specific everyday verb when context makes the intended result clear.

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [**Get It**: Understand](01-get-it-meaning-understand.md) | Al principio no entendía el chiste, pero ahora sí lo entiendo. | I didn't get the joke at first, but now I get it. |
| [**Get Something To Someone**](02-get-something-to-someone-or-somewhere.md) | Te enviaré el informe mañana y haré que los originales lleguen a la oficina. | I'll get the report to you tomorrow and get the originals to the office. |

## Mastery Phrase

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Al principio no lo entendía, luego lo entendí y ahora lo tengo claro; te lo haré llegar mañana. | I didn't get it at first, then I got it, and now I've got it; I'll get it to you tomorrow. |

# **Got**: Simple Past

**Get** is irregular: its simple-past form is **got**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ayer recibí tres mensajes, conseguí una cita y compré las entradas. | Yesterday I got three messages, got an appointment, and got the tickets. |

The repeated **got** naturally covers receive, obtain, and buy.

# **Gotten**: Past Participle

In American English, many receive and obtain meanings use **get → got → gotten** in perfect forms.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| He recibido tres mensajes y por fin he conseguido una cita. | I've gotten three messages and have finally gotten an appointment. |

British English normally uses **got** instead. American **have got** is also preserved in possession and obligation patterns, which belong to later parts of the map.

# Pronunciation: **Get, Got**, and **Gotten**

**Get** has `/e/`, **got** has `/ɑ/` in common American pronunciation, and **gotten** adds an unstressed final syllable. None has a common homophone.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Conseguí lo que recibí, pero todavía no he conseguido lo que quería obtener. | I got what I received, but I haven't gotten what I wanted to get yet. |

The intentionally repetitive sentence contrasts present **get**, past **got**, and participle **gotten**.

# Forms and Sounds of **Get**

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [**Got**: Simple Past](01-got-simple-past.md) | Ayer recibí tres mensajes, conseguí una cita y compré las entradas. | Yesterday I got three messages, got an appointment, and got the tickets. |
| [**Gotten**: Past Participle](02-gotten-past-participle.md) | He recibido tres mensajes y por fin he conseguido una cita. | I've gotten three messages and have finally gotten an appointment. |
| [Pronunciation: **Get, Got**, and **Gotten**](03-pronunciation-get-got-and-gotten.md) | Conseguí lo que recibí, pero todavía no he conseguido lo que quería obtener. | I got what I received, but I haven't gotten what I wanted to get yet. |

## Mastery Phrase

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Obtengo lo que puedo, ayer obtuve lo que quería y últimamente he obtenido más. | I get what I can, I got what I wanted yesterday, and I've gotten more lately. |

# **I got to** → **pude**

Use **pude** for this get meaning in the context shown.

# **Get To** a Place

Conversational **get to + place** means arrive at or reach the destination: before, the person wasn't there; afterward, they were.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llegamos al aeropuerto justo antes de que cerraran la puerta. | We got to the airport just before they closed the gate. |

Compare **get to the airport**, **arrive at the airport**, and **reach the airport**. **Reach** takes no **to**.

# **Get Here, There**, and **Home**

Don't use **to** before **here, there**, or **home**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llegué aquí a las ocho, llegué allá al mediodía y llegué a casa después de las seis. | I got here at eight, got there at noon, and got home after six. |

Say **get here / there / home**, not *get to here / to there / to home*.

# **Get Up**

**Get up** means move from lying or sitting to an upright position. In a morning routine, it means leave the bed after waking.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me desperté a las seis, pero no me levanté de la cama hasta las seis y media. | I woke up at six, but I didn't get up until six thirty. |

**Wake up** is stop sleeping; **get up** is physically rise.

# **Get Down**

As movement, **get down** can mean descend, lower yourself, or move into a crouching position.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Bájate de la mesa y agáchate para que la pelota no te golpee. | Get down from the table and get down so the ball doesn't hit you. |

Vehicle exit normally uses **get out of** or **get off**, not general **get down**.

# **Get In** and **Get Into** a Car

Use **get in** without a named object and **get into + vehicle/place** when entering a car, taxi, or similarly enclosed vehicle.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Súbete al carro; tenemos que irnos ya. | Get in the car; we've gotta leave now. |

**Get into the car** is equally correct and emphasizes movement from outside to inside.

# **Get Out Of** a Car

Use **get out** without a named object and **get out of + vehicle/place** when leaving a car, taxi, or enclosed space.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nos bajamos del taxi frente al hotel. | We got out of the taxi in front of the hotel. |

The change is from inside to outside.

# **Get On** and **Get Onto** Public Transport

Use **get on/onto** for boarding a bus, train, plane, bicycle, motorcycle, or other transport you ride on or can move around inside.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Subimos al avión después de montar en el bus equivocado. | We got on the plane after getting on the wrong bus. |

**Onto** emphasizes the movement; **on** is the usual conversational choice.

# **Get Off** Public Transport

Use **get off** for leaving a bus, train, plane, bicycle, or similar transport.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nos bajamos del bus, pero olvidamos bajarnos del tren en nuestra estación. | We got off the bus, but we forgot to get off the train at our stop. |

Keep the contrast visible: **get in/out of a car** but **get on/off a bus**.

# Moving: Getting Up Use **get up** for rising from bed or from a seated or lying position. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | levantarse | **to get up** | **Me levanto a las seis todos los días.**
I get up at six every day. **Get up** is a two-word phrasal verb. Keep **up** with **get**.

# **Get** and Movement

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [**Get To** a Place](01-get-to-a-place.md) | Llegamos al aeropuerto antes de que cerraran la puerta. | We got to the airport before they closed the gate. |
| [**Get Here, There**, and **Home**](02-get-here-there-and-home.md) | Llegué aquí, llegué allá y finalmente llegué a casa. | I got here, got there, and finally got home. |
| [**Get Up**](03-get-up.md) | Me desperté a las seis, pero no me levanté hasta las seis y media. | I woke up at six, but I didn't get up until six thirty. |
| [**Get Down**](04-get-down.md) | Bájate de la mesa y agáchate. | Get down from the table and get down. |
| [**Get In/Into** a Car](05-get-in-and-into-a-car.md) | Súbete al carro; tenemos que irnos. | Get in the car; we've gotta leave. |
| [**Get Out Of** a Car](06-get-out-of-a-car.md) | Nos bajamos del taxi frente al hotel. | We got out of the taxi in front of the hotel. |
| [**Get On/Onto** Public Transport](07-get-on-and-onto-public-transport.md) | Subimos al avión después de montar en el bus equivocado. | We got on the plane after getting on the wrong bus. |
| [**Get Off** Public Transport](08-get-off-public-transport.md) | Nos bajamos del bus y luego del tren. | We got off the bus and then got off the train. |

## Mastery Phrases

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me levanté, subí al carro, llegué al aeropuerto, subí al avión y bajé en Medellín. | I got up, got into the car, got to the airport, got on the plane, and got off in Medellín. |
| Llegué aquí, llegué allá y llegué a casa sin usar **to**. | I got here, got there, and got home without using **to**. |

## Foundation Retrieval Lesson

- [Get up](09-foundation-get-up.md)

# **Get** Meaning Receive

Conversational **get** can mean that something is sent, given, or delivered to someone.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Recibí tu mensaje esta mañana, pero todavía no he recibido el archivo. | I got your message this morning, but I haven't gotten the file yet. |

Formal or careful English may prefer **receive**.

# **Get** Versus **Receive**

**Get** is the usual conversational choice; **receive** is more formal and focuses clearly on something arriving.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Recibimos muchas solicitudes, pero solo obtuvimos una respuesta oficial. | We got lots of applications, but we received only one official response. |

The meanings overlap heavily; tone and context usually determine the choice.

# **Get, Obtain**, and **Acquire**

**Get** is broad and conversational. **Obtain** sounds formal or procedural; **acquire** often suggests gaining something gradually, deliberately, or permanently.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Conseguimos el permiso, obtuvimos la licencia oficial y adquirimos el equipo necesario. | We got permission, obtained the official license, and acquired the necessary equipment. |

# **Get** Meaning Buy or Order

In everyday speech, **get** can mean buy, order, or choose something to consume.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Voy a comprar leche y pediré el pollo para el almuerzo. | I'm gonna get some milk, and I'll get the chicken for lunch. |

Context distinguishes shopping from ordering food.

# **Get Permission** and **Get Approval**

Use **get** for successfully receiving authorization.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tenemos que obtener permiso del propietario y la aprobación del banco. | We've gotta get the owner's permission and get approval from the bank. |

# **Get Access**

**Get access to** means obtain the ability or authorization to enter, see, or use something.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No pude acceder al documento hasta que me dieron la contraseña. | I couldn't get access to the document until I got the password. |

# **Get a Chance** or **Opportunity**

Use **get a chance/opportunity to + base verb** when someone receives an occasion to act.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Por fin tuve la oportunidad de hablar con la directora. | I finally got a chance to speak with the director. |

# **Get Information** or **an Answer**

Use **get** for obtaining facts, explanations, news, or a response.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No pude obtener una respuesta, pero conseguí la información que necesitaba. | I couldn't get an answer, but I got the information I needed. |

# **Get a Result, Grade**, or **Score**

Use **get** for a result produced by a process, test, game, or evaluation.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Obtuve un buen resultado, saqué una nota alta y conseguí diez puntos. | I got a good result, got a high grade, and got ten points. |

The exact Spanish verb changes, but conversational English can reuse **get**.

# **Get Paid**

**Get paid** means receive payment.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me pagan el último viernes de cada mes. | I get paid on the last Friday of every month. |

This pattern uses **get + past participle** and will also connect to the later change/passive system.

# **Get a Gift, Message**, or **Delivery**

Use **get** for things that arrive through giving, communication, or delivery.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Recibí un regalo, dos mensajes y una entrega inesperada esta mañana. | I got a gift, two messages, and an unexpected delivery this morning. |

# **Get Hold Of**

**Get hold of** can mean obtain something or successfully contact someone.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Por fin conseguí una copia del contrato, pero no pude comunicarme con el abogado. | I finally got hold of a copy of the contract, but I couldn't get hold of the lawyer. |

Context distinguishes physical possession from contact.

# **Get Your Hands On**

Informal **get your hands on** means manage to obtain something, especially something desirable or difficult to find.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Si logro conseguir una copia anticipada, te la prestaré. | If I can get my hands on an early copy, I'll lend it to you. |

# Sending and Receiving: Receiving, Obtaining, and Getting English **get** can correspond to **recibir**, **obtener**, or **conseguir**, depending on the context. ## Receiving something Use **receive** or the more conversational **get** when something arrives or someone gives it to you. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | recibir algo | **to receive something**, **to get something** | **Recibo el documento por correo electrónico.**
I receive the document by email. **I get the document by email** expresses the same core idea more conversationally. ## Obtaining something Use **obtain** or **get** when you acquire something. **Obtain** is more formal. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | obtener algo | **to obtain something**, **to get something** | **Obtengo una copia del documento en la recepción.**
I obtain a copy of the document at reception. **I get a copy at reception** is more common in everyday conversation. ## Getting something successfully Spanish **conseguir** often emphasizes finding, securing, or succeeding in obtaining something. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | conseguir algo | **to get something** | **Consigo una cita para el viernes después de llamar varias veces.**
I get an appointment for Friday after calling several times.

# **Get** Meaning Obtain or Receive

| Lesson | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| [Receive](01-get-meaning-receive.md) | Recibí tu mensaje, pero todavía no he recibido el archivo. | I got your message, but I haven't gotten the file yet. |
| [**Get** Versus **Receive**](02-get-versus-receive.md) | Recibimos muchas solicitudes, pero solo obtuvimos una respuesta oficial. | We got lots of applications, but we received only one official response. |
| [**Get, Obtain**, and **Acquire**](04-get-obtain-and-acquire.md) | Obtuvimos la licencia y adquirimos el equipo. | We obtained the license and acquired the equipment. |
| [Buy or Order](05-get-meaning-buy-or-order.md) | Voy a comprar leche y pediré el pollo. | I'm gonna get some milk and get the chicken. |
| [Permission and Approval](07-get-permission-and-approval.md) | Tenemos que obtener permiso y la aprobación del banco. | We've gotta get permission and get the bank's approval. |
| [Access](08-get-access.md) | No pude acceder al documento hasta que recibí la contraseña. | I couldn't get access to the document until I got the password. |
| [Chance or Opportunity](09-get-a-chance-or-opportunity.md) | Por fin tuve la oportunidad de hablar con la directora. | I finally got a chance to speak with the director. |
| [Information or an Answer](11-get-information-or-an-answer.md) | No obtuve una respuesta. | I didn't get an answer. |
| [Result, Grade, or Score](12-get-a-result-grade-or-score.md) | Obtuve un buen resultado y una nota alta. | I got a good result and a high grade. |
| [Paid](13-get-paid.md) | Me pagan el último viernes de cada mes. | I get paid on the last Friday of every month. |
| [Gift, Message, or Delivery](14-get-a-gift-message-or-delivery.md) | Recibí un regalo, dos mensajes y una entrega. | I got a gift, two messages, and a delivery. |
| [**Get Hold Of**](15-get-hold-of.md) | No pude comunicarme con el abogado. | I couldn't get hold of the lawyer. |

## Mastery Phrases

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Recibí el mensaje, compré las entradas y obtuve el trabajo. | I got the message, got the tickets, and got the job. |
| No pude comunicarme con el abogado para obtener su aprobación. | I couldn't get hold of the lawyer to get his approval. |

## Core Translation Bridge

- [Receive, obtain, and get](17-receive-obtain-and-get.md)

# **Get To Do**: Have the Opportunity

**Get to + verb** means have the opportunity or privilege to do something.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| En este trabajo puedo viajar y conocer a personas de todo el mundo. | In this job, I get to travel and meet people from all over the world. |

Here, **get to** doesn't mean obligation. It presents the action as something available, special, or enjoyable: **We get to leave early today!**

# **Got To Do**: Had the Opportunity

The past of opportunity **get to** is **got to**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ayer tuve la oportunidad de conocer a mi cantante favorita y hablar con ella. | Yesterday I got to meet my favorite singer and talk to her. |

The time context makes the completed opportunity clear: **Last year, we got to visit Cartagena.**

# **Have** and **Have Got** for Possession

For present possession, **have** and **have got** normally mean the same thing.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo dos entradas, así que tenemos la oportunidad de ver el concierto. | I've got two tickets, so we get to see the concert. |

- **I have two tickets.**
- **I've got two tickets.**

In **I've got**, **'ve** means **have**. Although **got** looks past, the complete expression describes what I possess now.

# **Have To, Have Got To**, and **Gotta**

**Have to** and **have got to** express necessity or obligation. In informal speech, **have got to** is often reduced to **gotta**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo que terminar esto hoy porque tenemos que enviarlo mañana. | I've gotta finish this today because we have to send it tomorrow. |

- **I have to do it.**
- **I've got to do it.**
- **I gotta do it.** — informal representation of speech

**Gotta** is useful in dialogue and casual messages, but use **have to** or **have got to** in formal writing.

Don't use **gotta** for possession: **I've got a ticket** means tengo una entrada; **I've gotta get a ticket** means tengo que conseguir una entrada.

# **I Got To Do It** Versus **I Gotta Do It**

These phrases look and sound very similar, but the clearest standard contrast is opportunity versus obligation.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ayer tuve la oportunidad de hacerlo; hoy me toca hacerlo. | Yesterday I got to do it; today I gotta do it. |

- **I got to do it.** — I had the opportunity to do it.
- **I gotta do it.** — I have to do it.

In careful speech, opportunity is often **got tə**, while obligation may compress into **gotta**. Real casual pronunciation can overlap, so context matters. The tongue twister fixes the meanings: **Yesterday I got to do it; today I gotta do it.**

# Having: **Have To** and **Have Got To** ## **Have to** Use **have to + base verb** for an obligation or something that is necessary. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | tener que hacer algo | **to have to do something** | **Tengo que hacerlo hoy.**
I have to do it today. ## **Have got to** In the present, **have got to** also expresses obligation. It commonly becomes shorter in speech: | Form | Use | |---|---| | **I have got to do it.** | full form | | **I've got to do it.** | standard contraction | | **I gotta do it.** | very informal spoken form | All three can express: **Tengo que hacerlo.** **I've** is the contraction of **I have**. **Gotta** represents the informal spoken reduction of **got to**; use **have got to** or **I've got to** in standard writing.
