# English **Real**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Is the story real? | ¿La historia es real? |
| The real problem is time. | El verdadero problema es el tiempo. |
| She is a real expert. | Es toda una experta. |
| For real? | ¿En serio? |

Existence uses **real**, truth or identity **verdadero**, emphasis a fuller phrase, and informal confirmation **en serio**.

# English **Realize**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I realized that I was wrong. | Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado. |
| She realized her goal. | Alcanzó su meta. |
| They made the plan a reality. | Hicieron realidad el plan. |
| The company carried out the project. | La empresa realizó el proyecto. |

English **realize** meaning become aware is **darse cuenta**, not Spanish **realizar**. Achievement and making something real use **alcanzar** or **hacer realidad**.

# **Really** Meaning Truly

Use **really** to ask whether something is true or to emphasize that it is true.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Laura de verdad renunció, o solo está pensando en irse? | Did Laura really quit, or is she only thinking about leaving? |

The question contrasts a real resignation with a possible plan, so **really** means **de verdad** or **realmente**.

# **Really?** as a Reaction

On its own, **Really?** can express surprise, doubt or interest. Its tone helps determine whether it sounds curious or skeptical.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —Conseguí el trabajo en Toronto. —¿En serio? ¡Felicitaciones! | “I got the job in Toronto.” “Really? Congratulations!” |

Here **Really?** means **¿En serio?** or **¿De verdad?**

# **Really** as an Intensifier

Before an adjective or adverb, **really** commonly means **muy** and expresses a strong degree.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Es muy importante verificar el número de cuenta porque no podremos cancelar la transferencia. | It's really important to verify the account number because we won't be able to cancel the transfer. |
| Es realmente difícil. | It is really difficult. |

The standard contractions **it's** and **won't** are natural in speech and informal writing. In this context, **really important** is stronger than **kind of important** and normally stronger than **pretty important**.

Depending on tone and context, Spanish may naturally use **muy importante**, **realmente importante** or occasionally **bastante importante**. Do not memorize **bastante** as the fixed translation of **really**.

# **Really + Verb**

Before a verb, **really** can intensify a feeling, desire, need or opinion. Spanish often uses **mucho**, not **muy**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me gusta mucho este apartamento, pero no puedo pagar el arriendo. | I really like this apartment, but I can't afford the rent. |

Use **I really like it → me gusta mucho**, not the unnatural literal translation *me muy gusta*.

# **Not Really**

**Not really** gives a softened or qualified negative answer. It often means **no mucho**, **en realidad no** or **no exactamente**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —¿Te gustó la película? —La verdad, no mucho; la historia era demasiado predecible. | “Did you like the movie?” “Not really; the story was too predictable.” |

The speaker answers no but makes the rejection less blunt.

# English **Receive**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I received your message. | Recibí tu mensaje. |
| She received a good grade. | Sacó una buena nota. |
| The hotel receives guests all night. | El hotel recibe huéspedes toda la noche. |
| The signal is not being received. | No se capta la señal. |

General reception uses **recibir**, while grades and electronic signals commonly use **sacar** and **captar**.

# **Remember → No Olvidar** Spanish can express an instruction to remember something through the negative bridge **no olvidar**. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | no olvidar [algo] | **to remember [something]** | **No olvides la cita de mañana.**
Remember tomorrow's appointment.

# **Remember → Acordarse de**

English **remember + object** can map to Spanish **acordarse de + object**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me acuerdo de su nombre. | I remember her name. |

Spanish requires both **se** and **de** with **acordarse de**.

# English **Report**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Report the problem to your manager. | Infórmale del problema a tu jefe. |
| She reported the theft to the police. | Denunció el robo ante la policía. |
| Report for work at eight. | Preséntate a trabajar a las ocho. |
| The newspaper reported that prices rose. | El periódico informó que subieron los precios. |

Providing information uses **informar**; reporting wrongdoing **denunciar**; presenting oneself **presentarse**.

# **Right** for Direction

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Gira a la derecha y busca la farmacia a tu derecha. | Turn right and look for the pharmacy on your right. |

Use **right** after a movement verb for direction and **on/to the right** for position.

# **Be Right**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La respuesta es correcta y tú tienes razón sobre la causa. | The answer is right, and you're right about the cause. |

English uses **be right** for both **ser correcto** and **tener razón**. It does not say *have reason* for agreeing that a person is correct.

# Human **Rights**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Toda persona tiene los mismos derechos humanos, incluido el derecho a la educación. | Everyone has the same human rights, including the right to education. |

A **right** can be something a person is legally or morally entitled to have or do.

# **Right Now, Right Here**, and **Right Away**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Necesito la respuesta aquí mismo, ahora mismo, así que envíamela de inmediato. | I need the answer right here, right now, so send it right away. |

**Right** adds precision or immediacy: **right now** means at this exact moment, **right here** means in this exact place, and **right away** means immediately.

# Homophones: **Right, Write, Rite**, and **Wright**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El dramaturgo escribirá a la derecha el nombre correcto del rito. | The playwright will write the right name of the rite on the right. |

**Right**, **write**, **rite**, and **wright** are pronounced `/raɪt/`. **Right** can mean *derecha*, *correcto*, or *derecho*; **write** means *escribir*; a **rite** is a formal ceremony. A **wright** is a maker or builder, but the word is now mainly seen in compounds such as **playwright** and in surnames.

# **Right** for Position

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| a la derecha | on the right |
| hacia la derecha | to the right |

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La oficina está a la derecha. | The office is on the right. |
| Ve hacia la derecha. | Go to the right. |

# **Run → Correr**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I run in the park every morning. | Corro en el parque todas las mañanas. |

For movement on foot, **run** becomes **correr**.

# **Run → Funcionar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The machine runs on batteries. | La máquina funciona con pilas. |

For machines, software, and systems, use **funcionar, operar**, or **ejecutarse**.

# **Run → Dirigir / Administrar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| She runs a small company. | Ella dirige una empresa pequeña. |

For managing an organization or activity, Spanish uses **dirigir, administrar, manejar**, or **gestionar**.

# **Run → Durar**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The movie runs for two hours. | La película dura dos horas. |

For duration, **run** becomes **durar**.

# **Run → Postularse / Lanzarse**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| He's running for mayor. | Se está postulando para alcalde. |

For electoral candidacy, use **postularse, presentarse**, or Colombian **lanzarse**.

# **Run → Correr / Fluir**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Water ran down the wall. | El agua corrió por la pared. |

For liquids, Spanish uses **correr, fluir**, or **salir**, depending on the path and source.

# **Run → Ir / Circular**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The buses run every ten minutes. | Los buses pasan cada diez minutos. |

For a scheduled route or service, Spanish commonly uses **pasar, circular, operar**, or **ir**.

# **Run Out → Acabarse / Quedarse Sin**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| We ran out of coffee. | Se nos acabó el café. / Nos quedamos sin café. |

**Run out of** means exhaust a supply: **acabarse** or **quedarse sin**.

I run in the park before work.

| At the same time, it is risky. | Al mismo tiempo, es arriesgado. |

Shared identity uses **mismo**, equality **igual**, indifference **dar igual**, and fixed time expressions **al mismo tiempo**.

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| The firefighter saved the child. | El bombero salvó al niño. |
| Save the file before closing it. | Guarda el archivo antes de cerrarlo. |

| This method saves time. | Este método ahorra tiempo. |
| The museum saved the old building. | El museo conservó el edificio antiguo. |

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|

# English **Sell**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|

**I send the document to Natalia.**

English **send** usually maps to **enviar**. When the focus is delivery, Spanish may use **hacer llegar**.

# Modern Uses of English **Shall**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Empezamos? | Shall we start? |
| Empezaremos de inmediato. | We shall begin immediately. |
| El contratista deberá entregar el informe el viernes. | The contractor shall submit the report on Friday. |

**Shall I/we...?** makes an offer or suggestion. Affirmative **shall** can express formal determination and appears in legal requirements. In everyday English, future necessity is normally **will have to**, not **shall**.

# English **Should**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| If you should need help, call me. | Si llegaras a necesitar ayuda, llámame. |

# Seeing: Showing Something to Somebody Use **show + somebody + something** or **show + something + to + somebody**. | Spanish | English | |---|---| | mostrarle algo a alguien | **to show somebody something** | **Le muestro la foto a Camila.**
I show Camila the photo. Both English patterns are possible: **I show Camila the photo.**
**I show the photo to Camila.**

# **Show** Evidence or a Result

When **show** means establish or make something clear, Spanish commonly uses **demostrar**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los resultados demuestran que el método funciona. | The results show that the method works. |

# **Show** Somebody How

When **show** means teach or demonstrate a procedure, Spanish commonly uses **enseñar** or **mostrar**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Le enseño a usar la aplicación. | I show her how to use the application. |

# Uses of **Show**

English **show** maps to **mostrar** for making something visible, **demostrar** for evidence, and **enseñar** for a procedure.

# **Side**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Este lado de la caja está mojado, pero el otro lado está seco. | This side of the box is wet, but the other side is dry. |

**Side** can name one of two contrasting parts, one face of an object, or an area next to something.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay una puerta a cada lado del pasillo. | There's a door on each side of the hallway. |
| Ana está a mi lado. | Ana is by my side. |

Use **on this/that side of** for a position: **on this side of the river**. Use **by someone's side** for a position next to that person.

# **Inside** and **Outside**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El interior de la caja está seco, pero la parte exterior está mojada. | The inside of the box is dry, but the outside is wet. |

In these nouns, **in + side** forms **inside**, the inner part, and **out + side** forms **outside**, the outer part.

The same words can describe position:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los niños están adentro y los perros están afuera. | The children are inside, and the dogs are outside. |

For the larger contrast among **in, inside, out**, and **outside**, see [**In/Inside** and **Out/Outside**](../in/01-inside-and-outside.md).

For parts relative to a center, see [**Inner, Outer, Upper**, and **Lower**](../../../transformations/-er/other-forms/README.md).

# **Upside** and **Downside**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La ventaja es el salario; la desventaja es el horario. | The upside is the salary; the downside is the schedule. |

The visible parts—**up + side** and **down + side**—make the contrast memorable. In this common figurative pair, **upside** means **advantage** and **downside** means **disadvantage**.

For the larger **up/down** map, see [**Upside** and **Downside**](../up/core-uses/04-upside-and-downside.md).

# The **Front Side** and the **Back Side**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Escriba su nombre en la parte delantera de la tarjeta y la fecha en la parte de atrás. | Write your name on the front side of the card and the date on the back side. |

**The front side** is the forward-facing or main face. **The back side** is the opposite face.

In many contexts, English naturally shortens these expressions to **the front** and **the back**:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La entrada está en la parte delantera del edificio y el jardín está en la parte de atrás. | The entrance is at the front of the building, and the garden is at the back. |

For the larger physical contrast, see [The **Back** and the **Front**](../back/core-picture/01-the-back-and-the-front.md).

# The **Other Side** and **Across**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El banco queda al otro lado de la calle, frente a la farmacia. | The bank is on the other side of the street, across from the pharmacy. |

Use **on the other side of** to name the opposite position. Use **across from** when two places or people face each other with a space between them.

For movement from one side to the other, use **across** without **from**:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Cruzamos la calle para llegar al banco. | We walked across the street to get to the bank. |

For an interior path versus a path over an area or surface, see [**Through** vs **Across**](../through/confusion-sets/04-through-vs-across.md).

# **By** and **Beside**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Siéntese junto a Ana, al lado de la ventana. | Sit by Ana, beside the window. |

For position, both **by** and **beside** can mean **al lado de** or **junto a**. **By** can also allow the looser meaning **cerca de**, while **beside** more directly presents two things next to each other.

For the contrast with **near** and **next to**, see [**By, Near**, and **Next To**](../by/confusion-sets/03-by-near-next-to.md).

# **Besides**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Además del salario, el trabajo ofrece seguro médico. | Besides the salary, the job offers health insurance. |

**Besides + thing/person** means **además de** or **aparte de**.

**Besides** can also introduce an additional reason or point:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No quiero ese trabajo; además, queda demasiado lejos. | I don't want that job; besides, it's too far away. |

This meaning is not physical: **besides** does not mean **al lado de**.

# **Since** With a Starting Time

Use **since + starting point** for a situation continuing from then until a later reference point.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Trabajo aquí desde 2022. | I've worked here since 2022. |

Use **for three years** for the duration, not the starting point.

# **Since** With a Complete Event

Use **since + complete event** to name when the continuing period began.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No la he visto desde que cambió de trabajo. | I haven't seen her since she changed jobs. |

# **For** Versus **Since**

**For** gives the length of time; **since** gives its starting point.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Vivo aquí desde 2020, así que llevo seis años en este barrio. | I've lived here since 2020, so I've been in this neighborhood for six years. |

# **Ever Since**

**Ever since** emphasizes that a situation has continued from its starting point.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Desde que tuve el accidente, siempre he tomado el bus. | I've taken the bus ever since I had the accident. |

# **Since Then**

**Since then** means from a previously mentioned time until now or another reference time.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Renuncié en enero y desde entonces trabajo por mi cuenta. | I quit in January, and I've worked for myself since then. |

# **It's Been...Since...**

Use **it's been + period + since + event** to measure the time after an event.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Han pasado dos años desde que nos vimos. | It's been two years since we saw each other. |

English normally uses the simple past after **since** in this pattern.

# **Since** Meaning **Because**

At the beginning of a reason, **since** can mean **because**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ya que estamos aquí, mejor esperemos un rato. | Since we're already here, we might as well wait for a while. |

Use **because** when the reason needs stronger emphasis or **since** could sound temporal.

# **Since When?**

**Since when?** asks when a situation began and often expresses surprise.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Desde cuándo te gusta levantarte a las cinco? | Since when have you liked getting up at five? |

Informal **Since when do you like...?** is also common.

# **Long Since**

Formal **long since** means a long time ago or for a long time already.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ese sistema quedó obsoleto hace mucho tiempo. | That system has long since become obsolete. |

# **Not Since...**

**Not since + time/event** emphasizes that something hasn't happened during the whole period.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No había visto una tormenta así desde que era niña. | I hadn't seen a storm like that since I was a child. |

# **Since the Last Time**

Use **since the last time + complete idea** to compare the present with the most recent previous occasion.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El barrio ha cambiado mucho desde la última vez que vine. | The neighborhood's changed a lot since the last time I came. |

# Homophones: **Since** and **Sins**

**Since** and plural **sins** are homophones.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Desde que confesó sus pecados, no ha vuelto a mentir. | Since he confessed his sins, he hasn't lied again. |

Context and spelling distinguish the time/reason word from the plural noun.

# **So** Meaning **Tan**

Use **so** before a description to express a strong degree.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La película fue tan divertida que la vimos dos veces. | The movie was so funny that we watched it twice. |
| Es tan fácil. | It is so easy. |

The common pattern **so...that** connects the strong degree with its result: it was **so funny that** they watched it again.

# **So Much** and **So Many**

Spanish provides the direct distinction:

- **tanto trabajo → so much work**
- **tantos correos → so many emails**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo tanto trabajo y tantos correos pendientes que no podré salir temprano. | I've got so much work and so many unanswered emails that I won't be able to leave early. |

**I've** and **won't** are standard contractions. The separate intensifier contrast lesson compares **so much/many** with **too much/many**, **not that much/many** and **as much/many as**.

# **So** Meaning **Así Que**

Use **so** to introduce a result or consequence.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Había demasiado tráfico, así que llegamos veinte minutos tarde. | There was too much traffic, so we arrived twenty minutes late. |

The traffic caused the late arrival. This **so** connects two complete ideas.

# Sentence-Opening **So**

At the beginning of a sentence, **so** can introduce a conclusion, the next step or a new question. Spanish often uses **entonces**, **bueno** or no separate word.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Entonces, ya revisamos los costos. ¿Qué vamos a hacer ahora? | So, we've reviewed the costs. What are we going to do now? |

This conversational **so** organizes the discussion; it does not mean **tan**.

# Purpose: **So That**

Use **so that** for **para que** when an action is intended to produce a result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hablo despacio para que todos puedan entenderme. | I speak slowly so that everyone can understand me. |

In conversation, **that** is often omitted: **I speak slowly so everyone can understand me.**

Accented **¿para qué?** asks about purpose and is normally **what for?** or **why?**, not **so**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —Necesito otra llave. —¿Para qué? | “I need another key.” “What for?” |

# Agreement: **So Am I, So Do I, So Can I**

Use **so + helping verb + person** to agree with a positive statement.

| First statement | Agreement |
|---|---|
| **I'm tired.** | **So am I.** |
| **I work from home.** | **So do I.** |
| **I can drive.** | **So can I.** |
| **I'll attend.** | **So will I.** |
| **I've finished.** | **So have I.** |

Repeat the helping verb from the first statement. When the first statement has no visible helping verb, use **do**: **I work from home → So do I**.

Spanish **yo también** can also become **me too** in informal conversation. Compare:

- **So do I / Me too → Yo también.**
- **I also do it → También lo hago.**

The second sentence says that the speaker performs the same action; it is not the short agreement pattern.

For agreement with a negative statement, use **neither** instead: **I can't drive. Neither can I.**

# **I Think So**

After verbs such as **think**, **hope**, **suppose** and **guess**, **so** can replace a complete idea that is already understood.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —¿Va a aprobar Laura el examen? —Creo que sí; estudió toda la semana. | “Will Laura pass the exam?” “I think so; she studied all week.” |

**I think so** means **creo que sí** or, literally as a teaching bridge, **creo que es así**. It is more natural than repeating **I think Laura will pass the exam**.

Use **I think it's like that** only when **like that** describes a manner, arrangement or process.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Creo que el sistema funciona así, pero revisemos el manual para estar seguros. | I think the system works like that, but let's check the manual to be sure. |

# **I Don't Think So**

Use **I don't think so** for **no lo creo** or **creo que no**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —¿Está abierto el banco hoy? —No lo creo; hoy es festivo. | “Is the bank open today?” “I don't think so; today's a holiday.” |

**I don't think it's like that** refers more literally to the manner or situation being “like that.” It is not the normal replacement for **I don't think so**.

# **If So**

**If so** means **si es así**, **en ese caso** or **si la respuesta es sí**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿El cliente ya aprobó el diseño? Si es así, podemos publicarlo hoy. | Has the client approved the design? If so, we can publish it today. |

Here **so** replaces the complete idea **the client has approved the design**.

# **So?** and **So What?**

On its own, **So?** asks for the consequence or relevance of what was just said. **So what?** dismisses that information more strongly.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —El competidor tiene una oficina más grande. —¿Y qué? La nuestra atiende a más clientes. | “The competitor has a larger office.” “So what? Ours serves more clients.” |

Depending on tone, **So?** can mean **¿y?**, **¿entonces?** or **¿y eso qué?** Spanish *¿así qué?* is not the natural translation of **So what?**

# **So Far**

**So far** means **hasta ahora** when referring to progress up to the present.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hasta ahora hemos migrado todas las lecciones previstas para esta semana. | So far, we've migrated every lesson planned for this week. |

The common response **so far, so good** means **hasta ahora, todo bien**.

In a distance context, **so far** can instead mean **tan lejos**: **I didn't expect us to walk so far → No esperaba que camináramos tan lejos**.

# **Or So** Meaning Approximately

After a number or amount, **or so** means **aproximadamente**, **más o menos** or **unos/unas**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La reparación tardará unas dos semanas. | The repair will take two weeks or so. |

Use **or something like that** for an approximate description: **It was a warning or something like that → Era una advertencia o algo así**. The two expressions overlap only when approximation is involved.

# **And So On**

**And so on** continues an obvious list and means **etcétera**, **y así sucesivamente** or **y demás**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El formulario pide el nombre, la dirección, el teléfono y demás. | The form asks for your name, address, phone number, and so on. |

Use it only when the listener can reasonably infer the omitted items.

# **So-Called**

**So-called** introduces the name people give someone or something. It can be neutral, but it often signals doubt or criticism.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El supuesto experto no pudo responder ninguna pregunta básica. | The so-called expert couldn't answer a single basic question. |

The skeptical context makes **so-called** equivalent to **supuesto** here.

# **So-So**

Informal **so-so** means neither good nor bad.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —¿Cómo estuvo la comida? —Regular; el plato principal estaba frío. | “How was the food?” “So-so; the main course was cold.” |

# Homophones: **So, Sew** and **Sow**

**So**, **sew** and the verb **sow** are pronounced `/soʊ/`.

- **so** performs the functions taught in this lesson;
- **sew** means **coser**;
- **sow** means **sembrar**.

The noun **sow**, meaning an adult female pig, is a heteronym pronounced `/saʊ/`.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Coso tantas bolsas y siembro tantas semillas que termino muy cansada. | I sew so many bags and sow so many seeds that I end up so tired. |

| Spanish | English |

So far, we've fixed the budget, the schedule, and so on.” |

# **Some** With More Than One Thing

Use **some + plural things** for an unspecified number greater than zero.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Compré unos libros para la clase. | I bought some books for the class. |

# **Some** With Part of an Amount

Use **some** for an unspecified part or quantity.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Leí parte del libro y tomé un poco de café. | I read some of the book and had some coffee. |

# **Some Of**

Use **some of + known group or amount**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Algunos de los libros estaban dañados. | Some of the books were damaged. |

Use **some books** for an unidentified group and **some of the books** for part of a known group.

# **Some** in Offers and Requests

Questions often use **some** when offering something or requesting something expected.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Quieres un poco de café? ¿Me puedes prestar algo de dinero? | Would you like some coffee? Could you lend me some money? |

Neutral information questions generally use **any**.

# **Some** Versus **Any**

**Some** is common in positive statements; **any** is common in neutral questions and negatives.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo algunos libros, pero no tengo ninguno sobre ese tema. | I've got some books, but I don't have any on that topic. |

# **Someone, Something**, and **Somewhere**

The **some-** compounds refer to an unidentified person, thing, or place.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Alguien dejó algo en algún lugar de la oficina. | Someone left something somewhere in the office. |

# **Some** Versus **Same**

**Some** means an unspecified amount or number; **same** means identical or unchanged.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Algunos estudiantes dieron la misma respuesta de siempre. | Some students gave the same answer as always. |

They aren't homophones: **some** has `/ʌ/`; **same** has `/eɪ/`.

# **Sometimes, Sometime**, and **Some Time**

**Sometimes** means occasionally, **sometime** means at an unspecified time, and **some time** means a period.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A veces practico sola; deberíamos reunirnos algún día y dedicar algo de tiempo a practicar. | Sometimes I practice alone; we should meet sometime and spend some time practicing. |

# **Somehow**

**Somehow** means in an unknown way or despite difficulty.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| De alguna manera, logramos terminar a tiempo. | Somehow, we managed to finish on time. |

# **Somewhere, Anywhere, Nowhere**, and **Everywhere**

Use this family to talk about places without naming the place.

| Form | Core meaning | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| somewhere | an unspecified place | Laura está en algún lugar tranquilo. | Laura is somewhere quiet. |
| anywhere | a place in a question or negative | ¿Podemos reunirnos en algún lugar? | Can we meet anywhere? |
| nowhere | no place | No hay dónde sentarse. | There is nowhere to sit. |
| everywhere | every place | Busqué las llaves por todas partes. | I looked everywhere for the keys. |

In ordinary negative English, use either **not + anywhere** or **nowhere**, not both:

- We **didn't go anywhere**.
- We **went nowhere**.
- Not: *We didn't go nowhere.*

**Anywhere** can also mean any possible place:

**Puedes sentarte en cualquier lugar. → You can sit anywhere.**

All four place compounds are written as one word.

# Emphatic **Some**

Informal emphatic **some** can mark something as remarkable, often with an approving or ironic tone.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¡Esa sí que fue una reunión! Duró cinco horas. | That was some meeting! It lasted five hours. |

Tone determines whether the reaction is impressed or critical.

# **Sometime, No Time**, and **Every Time**

| Form | Core meaning | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| sometime | at an unspecified time | Llámame algún día la próxima semana. | Call me sometime next week. |
| no time | no available time | Hoy no tengo tiempo para almorzar. | I have no time for lunch today. |
| every time | on every occasion | Ella sonríe cada vez que escucha la canción. | She smiles every time she hears the song. |

## Spelling contrasts

- **sometime** = at an unspecified time: **Let's meet sometime.**
- **some time** = a period of time: **The repair will take some time.**
- **sometimes** = on some occasions: **I sometimes walk to work.**

Always write **no time** and **every time** as two words. Do not write *notime* or *everytime*.

# Homophones: **Some** and **Sum**

**Some** and **sum**, a total in mathematics, are homophones.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Algunos estudiantes calcularon la misma suma de varias maneras. | Some students calculated the same sum in several ways. |

The sentence also keeps **some** distinct from the near-sounding **same**.

# Related Pronouns: **Some, Any, No**, and **Every**

The determiner families also build indefinite pronouns.

| Family | Spanish: people | English: people | Spanish: things | English: things |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| some | alguien | somebody / someone | algo | something |
| any | alguien...? | anybody / anyone | algo...? | anything |
| no | nadie | nobody / no one | nada | nothing |
| every | todo el mundo / todos | everybody / everyone | todo | everything |

Compare:

| With a noun: determiner | Without a noun: pronoun |
|---|---|
| some person | somebody |
| any object | anything |
| no person | nobody |
| every object | everything |

The compounds are written as one word except **no one**.

In questions, Spanish can use **alguien** or **algo** where English normally uses the **any** family:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Hay alguien aquí? | Is anybody here? |
| ¿Necesitas algo? | Do you need anything? |

In ordinary negative English, use **not + any** or a negative pronoun, not both:

- **I don't know anybody.**
- **I know nobody.**
- Not: *I don't know nobody.*

Continue with the focused [people](19-indefinite-pronouns-people.md) and [things](20-indefinite-pronouns-things.md) lessons. The related source families are indexed under [**any**](../any/README.md), [**no**](../no/README.md), and [**every**](../every/README.md).

Learn this sequence as one complete pattern.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **Creo que hay alguien en la casa.** | I think somebody is in the house. |
| **¿Hay alguien en la casa?** | Is anybody in the house? |
| **Nadie está en la casa.** | Nobody is in the house. |
| **No hay nadie en la casa.** | There isn't anybody in the house. |
| **No creo que haya nadie en la casa.** | I don't think anybody is in the house. |
| **Cualquiera puede entrar en la casa.** | Anybody can enter the house. |
| **Todo el mundo está en la casa.** | Everybody is in the house. |

## Pattern

| Context | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | **alguien** | somebody / someone |
| Question | **alguien** | anybody / anyone |
| Negative pronoun | **nadie** | nobody / no one |
| Negative sentence | **no...nadie** | not anybody / not anyone |
| Any possible person | **cualquiera** | anybody / anyone |
| All people | **todo el mundo** | everybody / everyone |

# Things: Something, Anything, Nothing and Everything

Learn this sequence as one complete pattern.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **Creo que hay algo en la caja.** | I think something is in the box. |
| **¿Hay algo en la caja?** | Is there anything in the box? |
| **Nada está en la caja.** | Nothing is in the box. |
| **No hay nada en la caja.** | There isn't anything in the box. |
| **No creo que haya nada en la caja.** | I don't think anything is in the box. |
| **Puedes poner cualquier cosa en la caja.** | You can put anything in the box. |
| **Todo está en la caja.** | Everything is in the box. |

## Pattern

| Context | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | **algo** | something |
| Question | **algo** | anything |
| Negative pronoun | **nada** | nothing |
| Negative sentence | **no...nada** | not anything |
| Any possible thing | **cualquier cosa** | anything |
| All things | **todo** | everything |

# Indefinite Pronouns: People

These pronouns refer to people without identifying exactly who they are.

## Core forms

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **alguien** | somebody / someone |
| **todo el mundo** | everybody / everyone |
| **todos / todas** | everybody / everyone |
| **nadie** | nobody / no one |
| **cualquiera** | anybody / anyone |

## Somebody / Someone

**Alguien está en la casa.**  
Somebody is in the house. / Someone is in the house.

## Everybody / Everyone

**Todo el mundo está listo.**  
Everybody is ready. / Everyone is ready.

**Todos están listos.**  
Everybody is ready. / Everyone is ready.

- **Todo el mundo** uses a singular verb.
- **Todos / todas** uses a plural verb.

## Nobody / No one

**Nadie está en la casa.**  
Nobody is in the house. / No one is in the house.

## Anybody / Anyone in questions

Spanish normally uses **alguien** when asking whether a person exists:

**¿Hay alguien en la casa?**  
Is anybody in the house? / Is anyone in the house?

## Anybody / Anyone in negative sentences

Spanish uses **nadie**:

**No veo a nadie.**  
I do not see anybody. / I do not see anyone.

## Anybody / Anyone meaning “any person”

Use **cualquiera** when every person is a possible option:

**Cualquiera puede aprender inglés.**  
Anybody can learn English. / Anyone can learn English.

## The personal **a**

Use **a** when these pronouns are the direct object of a verb:

- **Veo a alguien.** — I see somebody.
- **No veo a nadie.** — I do not see anybody.
- **Conozco a todo el mundo.** — I know everybody.

## Negative word order

If **nadie** comes before the verb, do not use **no**:

**Nadie vino.**  
Nobody came.

If **nadie** comes after the verb, use **no**:

**No vino nadie.**  
Nobody came.

## Adding **else**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **alguien más** | somebody else / someone else |
| **nadie más** | nobody else / no one else |

**Necesitamos a alguien más.**  
We need somebody else.

# Indefinite Pronouns: Things

These pronouns refer to things without identifying exactly what they are.

## Core forms

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **algo** | something |
| **todo** | everything |
| **nada** | nothing |
| **cualquier cosa** | anything |

## Something

**Hay algo en la caja.**  
There is something in the box.

## Everything

**Todo está listo.**  
Everything is ready.

## Nothing

**Nada funciona.**  
Nothing works.

## Anything in questions

Spanish normally uses **algo** when asking whether a thing exists:

**¿Quieres algo?**  
Do you want anything?

## Anything in negative sentences

Spanish uses **nada**:

**No quiero nada.**  
I do not want anything.

## Anything meaning “any possible thing”

Use **cualquier cosa** when every option is possible:

**Puedes elegir cualquier cosa.**  
You can choose anything.

## Negative word order

If **nada** comes before the verb, do not use **no**:

**Nada funciona.**  
Nothing works.

If **nada** comes after the verb, use **no**:

**No funciona nada.**  
Nothing works.

## Adjectives come after the pronoun

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **algo interesante** | something interesting |
| **todo importante** | everything important |
| **nada nuevo** | nothing new |

**Quiero aprender algo nuevo.**  
I want to learn something new.

## Adding **else**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| **algo más** | something else |
| **nada más** | nothing else |

**¿Quieres algo más?**  
Do you want anything else?

| Espero con ilusión conocerlos el lunes. | I look forward to meeting you on Monday. |

**Look forward to** means await something with pleasure or anticipation, not physically look ahead. Because **to** is part of this fixed connection, use a noun or an **-ing** form after it: **our meeting** or **meeting you**, not *meet you*.

# **Can't Wait**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo muchas ganas de verlos; ¡no veo la hora! | I can't wait to see you! |

**Can't wait to** expresses strong, enthusiastic anticipation and is more informal than **look forward to**. It normally takes **to + base verb**: **can't wait to see**, not *can't wait to seeing*.

# Homophones: **Straight** and **Strait**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El barco siguió derecho por el estrecho angosto. | The ship went straight through the narrow strait. |

**Straight** and **strait** are pronounced `/streɪt/`. **Straight** means direct or without curves; a **strait** is a narrow waterway between two land areas.

# **Forward** and **Forwards**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Mire hacia adelante y dé dos pasos hacia adelante. | Look forward and take two steps forwards. |

**Forward** and **forwards** mark direction toward the front. **Forwards** is especially common in British English; **forward** is standard in both British and American English.

Only **forward** normally goes before a noun: **a forward movement**, not *a forwards movement*.

For a physical gaze, **look forward** means look ahead. The fixed connection **look forward to** has the different meaning **esperar con ilusión**.

See the productive transformation under [**-ward**](../../../transformations/-ward/06-forward-and-forwards.md).

# **Straight Ahead**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| derecho / todo recto | straight ahead |

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Sigue derecho. | Go straight ahead. |

# **Derecho**: **Straight** or **Right**?

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Sigue derecho dos cuadras y después gira a la derecha. | Go straight for two blocks and then turn right. |

In directions, Colombian Spanish distinguishes **derecho** for continuing straight from **a la derecha** for turning right. English cannot use **right** for both: **go straight**, but **turn right**.

Achieve result.

# **Such** Meaning That Kind

Use **such + noun** for something of the kind just mentioned.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nunca había visto tal confusión en una reunión tan corta. | I'd never seen such confusion in such a short meeting. |

# **Such a + Description + Singular Thing**

Use **such a/an + description + singular thing**. **So** goes directly before the description.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ella es una mujer tan paciente porque ha tenido una vida muy difícil. | She's such a patient woman because she's had such a difficult life. |

Compare **She's so patient** with **She's such a patient woman**.

# **Such** With Plural or Uncountable Things

Don't use **a/an** before plural or uncountable things.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nunca habíamos recibido consejos tan útiles ni instrucciones tan claras. | We'd never received such useful advice or such clear instructions. |

# **Such As**

Use **such as** to introduce examples.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Necesitamos documentos tales como el pasaporte y el certificado bancario. | We need documents such as your passport and bank certificate. |

# **There's No Such Thing As**

Use **there's no such thing as...** to say that an idea or thing doesn't exist.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No existe tal cosa como una contraseña completamente imposible de descifrar. | There's no such thing as a completely unbreakable password. |

# **Such...That**

Use **such + noun phrase + that + result** when a quality or degree produces a consequence.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue una reunión tan larga que tuvimos que pedir la cena. | It was such a long meeting that we had to order dinner. |

# **Such and Such**

Informal **such and such** replaces a name or detail that is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately omitted.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dijo que nos reuniéramos con cierta persona en cierto lugar, pero no dio detalles claros. | He said to meet so-and-so at such-and-such a place, but he didn't give clear details. |

# **As Such**

**As such** can mean in that exact role or therefore because of that role.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Laura es la gerente y, como tal, tiene que aprobar el presupuesto. | Laura's the manager and, as such, has to approve the budget. |

Don't use **as such** as a vague replacement for **therefore** unless the preceding role clearly supports it.

# **Such Is...**

Formal **such is/are...** means that is the nature or result of something.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Así es la vida: a veces el mejor plan no funciona. | Such is life: sometimes the best plan doesn't work. |

# Pronunciation: **Such** and **Suck**

**Such** ends in `/tʃ/`; **suck** ends in `/k/`. They aren't homophones.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Un cambio tan repentino puede hacer que una bomba succione demasiado aire. | Such a sudden change can make a pump suck in too much air. |

The sentence deliberately repeats the short vowel while contrasting the endings.

# English **Than**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Laura is taller than Mateo. | Laura es más alta que Mateo. |
| I have more than ten dollars. | Tengo más de diez dólares. |
| It cost less than expected. | Costó menos de lo esperado. |
| Rather than wait, we left. | En vez de esperar, nos fuimos. |

Comparison with a person or thing usually uses **que**; comparison before a number uses **de**. **Than expected** and **rather than** require complete expressions.

# English **Thank**

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| Thank Laura for her help. | Agradécele a Laura su ayuda. |
| Thank you for coming. | Gracias por venir. |
| I have you to thank for this opportunity. | Te debo esta oportunidad. |

Verb **thank** uses **agradecer**, the routine expression uses **gracias**, and assigning positive credit may use **deber**.

# **That + Thing**

Use **that** before one person or thing that is distant, already identified, or being contrasted with something nearer.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ese libro que está junto a la ventana es el que necesito. | That book by the window is the one I need. |

The basic set is:

| Distance | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| nearer | **this book** | **these books** |
| farther | **that book** | **those books** |

Distance can be physical, temporal, emotional or conversational: **that day**, **that problem**, **that idea you mentioned**.

# **That** Standing Alone

**That** can replace a singular thing or complete idea already visible or understood.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me gusta eso, pero no me gusta aquello que está junto a la puerta. | I like that, but I don't like that one by the door. |

**That one** emphasizes a choice among similar items. Plural **those** normally stands alone without **ones**: **I like those**.

# **That** Versus **It**

Use **that** to point, identify, contrast, or react to a newly mentioned idea. Use **it** to continue referring neutrally to something already established.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| —Compré una bicicleta nueva. —¡Eso es genial! ¿Cuándo la vas a usar? | “I bought a new bicycle.” “That's great! When are you going to use it?” |

**That** reacts to the news; **it** then refers to the bicycle.

# Connector **That** After Thinking and Speaking

Use **that** to introduce a complete idea after verbs such as **think, believe, know, say, explain, notice, remember**, and **hope**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Creo que Laura sabe que la reunión empieza a las nueve. | I think that Laura knows that the meeting starts at nine. |

This **that** does not point to an object. It introduces what someone thinks or knows.

# Optional Connector **That**

In everyday English, connector **that** is often omitted.

| With **that** | Without **that** |
|---|---|
| **I think that Laura is right.** | **I think Laura is right.** |
| **She said that she'd call.** | **She said she'd call.** |
| **We know that it works.** | **We know it works.** |

Keep **that** when it makes a long sentence easier to read or prevents the first words of the new idea from being mistaken for part of the earlier phrase.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El gerente confirmó que los cambios que solicitó el cliente estarán listos mañana. | The manager confirmed that the changes the client requested will be ready tomorrow. |

The first **that** clearly opens the confirmed idea; the second relative **that** has been omitted after **changes**.

# Connector **That** After a Description

**That** can introduce the idea connected to a reaction, certainty or evaluation.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estoy segura de que el archivo está listo y me alegra que Laura lo haya revisado. | I'm sure that the file is ready, and I'm glad that Laura reviewed it. |

Common chunks include **be sure that**, **be aware that**, **be glad that**, **be sorry that**, and **be surprised that**. In conversation, **that** is often omitted: **I'm sure it's ready**.

# Noun + Connector **That**

After a noun, **that** can explain the content of a fact, idea, claim, possibility, evidence, news or belief.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La posibilidad de que el vuelo sea cancelado cambia nuestro plan. | The possibility that the flight will be canceled changes our plan. |

Compare content **that** with relative **that**:

- **the news that Laura resigned**: the news is “Laura resigned”;
- **the news that surprised us**: the news performed the action **surprised**.

# When Spanish **Que** Does Not Become Connector **That**

After verbs such as **want, need, ask**, and **tell**, English often uses **person + to + base verb**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quiero que Laura lo haga y necesito que Carlos la ayude. | I want Laura to do it, and I need Carlos to help her. |

Do not say *I want that Laura does it* in the standard pattern taught here.

# **That** Versus **So** After **Think**

**I think that...** introduces the idea. **I think so** replaces an idea already understood.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Creo que Laura va a ganar. | I think that Laura will win. |
| —¿Va a ganar Laura? —Creo que sí. | “Will Laura win?” “I think so.” |

**I think it's like that** means **creo que es así** when describing a manner, arrangement or process.

# Relative **That**

Relative **that** connects a person or thing to information needed to identify it.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Necesito algo que funcione sin internet y una persona que pueda instalarlo. | I need something that works without internet and someone who can install it. |

**That** is natural for things and possible for people. **Who** is usually the more natural choice for people.

# Relative **That** Versus **Which**

Use **that** or **which** for information that identifies which thing you mean.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El archivo que contiene las cifras definitivas está en esta carpeta. | The file that contains the final figures is in this folder. |

For extra, non-identifying information after a comma, use **which**, not **that**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El archivo final, que enviamos ayer, contiene las cifras corregidas. | The final file, which we sent yesterday, contains the corrected figures. |

The comma signals that **we sent yesterday** adds extra information; it does not identify the already specific final file.

# When Relative **That** Can Disappear

Omit relative **that** when another person or thing performs the following action.

| With **that** | Without **that** |
|---|---|
| **The book that I need** | **The book I need** |
| **The change that Laura requested** | **The change Laura requested** |

Do not omit **that** when **that** itself performs the action:

- **The book that is on the table**
- not *The book is on the table* when it must remain part of a larger phrase.

Compare:

- **the file (that) Laura sent**: Laura sent the file, so **that** can disappear;
- **the file that contains the figures**: the file contains the figures, so **that** stays.

# Prepositions and Relative **That**

Conversational English commonly leaves the preposition at the end:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esa es la persona con la que hablé y el tema al que me referí. | That's the person that I spoke to and the topic that I referred to. |

In formal fronted patterns, use **whom** or **which**, not **that**:

- **the person to whom I spoke**
- **the topic to which I referred**
- not *the person to that I spoke*.

# **Not That + Description**

Use **not that** to reject or lower a degree that someone expects.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El examen no estuvo tan difícil; terminé veinte minutos antes. | The exam wasn't that difficult; I finished twenty minutes early. |

The direct patterns are:

- **no tan ocupado → not that busy**
- **no tanto tráfico → not that much traffic**
- **no tantos carros → not that many cars**

# Positive Degree **That**

In questions, conditions and comparisons, **that** can mean **tan** or **así de** by referring to a degree already understood.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿De verdad está así de lejos? Si queda tan lejos, tomemos un taxi. | Is it really that far? If it's that far, let's take a taxi. |

Informal **I didn't know it was that expensive** means the price was higher than the speaker expected.

# **So...That**

In **so + description + that + result**, **so** expresses the degree and **that** introduces its consequence.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Estaba tan cansada que se quedó dormida en el bus. | She was so tired that she fell asleep on the bus. |

In conversation, result **that** can sometimes disappear: **She was so tired she fell asleep on the bus.**

# **Such...That**

Use **such + noun phrase + that + result** when the noun itself is central to the description.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue una reunión tan larga que tuvimos que pedir la cena. | It was such a long meeting that we had to order dinner. |

Compare:

- **The meeting was so long that...**
- **It was such a long meeting that...**

# Purpose **So That**

**So that** commonly translates **para que**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Te envío las dos versiones para que puedas compararlas. | I'm sending you both versions so that you can compare them. |

Conversational English often omits **that**: **I'm sending both versions so you can compare them.**

# **Like That** and **That Way**

**Like that** and **that way** can mean **así**, **de esa manera** or **de ese modo**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No organices los archivos así; si lo haces de esa manera, nadie podrá encontrarlos. | Don't organize the files like that; if you do it that way, nobody will be able to find them. |

Use **it is like that** to describe what something is like. Use **it works that way** to describe how it operates.

# **At That Time**

**At that time** means **en ese momento** or **en aquella época**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| En aquella época trabajaba de noche, así que no podía asistir a las clases. | At that time, I worked nights, so I couldn't attend the classes. |

Depending on the timeline, natural alternatives include **then**, **back then**, and **at the time**.

# **Now That**

**Now that** introduces a changed circumstance and often means **ahora que** or **ya que ahora**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ahora que tenemos las cifras definitivas, podemos enviar el informe. | Now that we have the final figures, we can send the report. |

# Reason and Condition Expressions

Several expressions use **that** to introduce a reason, fact or condition:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dado que el cliente aprobó el diseño, podemos publicarlo. | Given that the client approved the design, we can publish it. |
| Considerando que es festivo, hay bastante tráfico. | Considering that it's a holiday, there's quite a lot of traffic. |
| Siempre que todos estén de acuerdo, firmaremos hoy. | Provided that everyone agrees, we'll sign today. |

**In that** gives a specific respect in which a statement is true:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los dos trabajos son parecidos porque ambos requieren contacto diario con clientes. | The two jobs are similar in that both require daily contact with clients. |

# **The Fact That**

Use **the fact that** when the reality of an idea is itself important.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El hecho de que Laura hablara con el cliente evitó otro retraso. | The fact that Laura spoke to the client prevented another delay. |

Do not add **the fact that** mechanically to every Spanish **el hecho de que** if a shorter sentence communicates the same idea clearly.

# **That's Why, That's How**, and **That's What**

These expressions connect a result, method or identification to the previous context.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Perdimos el último bus; por eso llegamos tarde. | We missed the last bus; that's why we were late. |
| Laura convirtió el archivo a PDF; así resolvió el problema. | Laura converted the file to PDF; that's how she solved the problem. |
| Necesito una respuesta clara; eso es lo que espero recibir. | I need a clear answer; that's what I expect to receive. |

**That's** is the standard contraction of **that is** or **that has**, depending on what follows: **That's important → that is**; **That's been difficult → that has**.

# **That's Why** Versus **That's Because**

**That's why** introduces a result. **That's because** introduces its cause.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El bus se averió; por eso llegamos tarde. | The bus broke down; that's why we were late. |
| Llegamos tarde porque el bus se averió. | We were late; that's because the bus broke down. |

Follow the direction of the explanation:

- cause → **that's why** → result;
- result → **that's because** → cause.

# Emphatic **It Is...That**

Use **it is/was + emphasized information + that...** to focus attention on one part of a sentence.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue Laura quien encontró el error, no Carlos. | It was Laura that found the error, not Carlos. |

**Who** is also natural for a person: **It was Laura who found the error**.

# **That's It, That's All**, and **That's That**

- **That's it** can identify the correct thing or announce completion.
- **That's all** means there is nothing more.
- **That's that** emphatically closes a discussion or decision.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esa es la llave que buscaba. Eso es todo; podemos irnos. | That's it—the key I was looking for. That's all; we can leave. |
| La decisión es definitiva y se acabó el asunto. | The decision is final, and that's that. |

# **That Is** and **That Is To Say**

Use **that is** or formal **that is to say** to clarify or restate something.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nos reuniremos el próximo día hábil, es decir, el lunes. | We'll meet on the next business day—that is, Monday. |

The abbreviation **i.e.** represents Latin *id est* and means **that is**, not **for example**.

# **That Said**

**That said** or **having said that** introduces a qualification or contrast with the previous statement.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El plan es costoso. Dicho esto, podría ahorrarnos dinero a largo plazo. | The plan is expensive. That said, it could save us money in the long run. |

# **And All That**

Informal **and all that** means **y todo eso**, **y demás** or **etcétera**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hablamos del presupuesto, del cronograma y todo eso. | We talked about the budget, the schedule, and all that. |

# **That Of** and **Those Of**

In formal comparisons, **that of** and **those of** prevent repetition.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El clima de Bogotá es más frío que el de Cartagena. | Bogotá's climate is colder than that of Cartagena. |
| Los costos de este año son mayores que los del año pasado. | This year's costs are higher than those of last year. |

Use singular **that of** for one repeated thing and plural **those of** for several.

# Pronunciation

Pointing or emphasized **that** normally has the strong vowel `/ðæt/`.

Connector and relative **that** are often unstressed and may reduce toward `/ðət/` in connected speech:

- strong: **I want THAT one.**
- reduced: **I think that it's ready.**

The initial `/ð/` is voiced: place the tongue lightly between the teeth and use the voice.

# No Common Homophone: **That, Than**, and **Then**

**That** has no common standard-English homophone. The useful sound-and-meaning contrast is with **than** and **then**:

| Word | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **that** | points or connects | **That book is the one that I need.** |
| **than** | comparison | **That book is better than this one.** |
| **then** | time or next step | **That book was cheaper then.** |

> **That was better than this then, but this is better than that now.**

# **The**

Use **the** when the listener can identify which person, thing, or group you mean.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| el gato | the cat |
| la tienda | the store |
| los gatos | the cats |
| las tiendas | the stores |

English **the** does not change for gender or number.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Quiero un libro. El libro está en la tienda. | I want a book. The book is at the store. |

The first mention introduces **a book**. The second uses **the book** because it is now identifiable.

# Translations of **Them**

This map collects the Spanish choices for English **them** according to object, indirect-object, and reflexive context.

# Uses of “Them”

English uses `them` for plural people, animals and objects.

Spanish changes the form depending on:

- whether `them` is a direct or indirect object;
- the grammatical gender of the people, animals or objects;
- whether the group is masculine, feminine or mixed;
- whether `them` follows a preposition;
- whether it identifies the recipient in a combined-pronoun construction.

# Direct Object

## Masculine or Mixed: Los

`Los` represents masculine plural direct objects and mixed groups.

| Reference | Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| 👨👨 los hombres | Veo a los hombres. | Los veo. | I see the men. I see them. |
| 👨👩 el hombre y la mujer | Veo al hombre y a la mujer. | Los veo. | I see the man and woman. I see them. |
| 🐕️🐕️ los perros | Veo a los perros. | Los veo. | I see the dogs. I see them. |
| 🤖🤖 los robots | Veo los robots. | Los veo. | I see the robots. I see them. |
| 📚️ los libros | Veo los libros. | Los veo. | I see the books. I see them. |

## Feminine: Las

`Las` represents feminine plural direct objects.

| Reference | Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| 👩👩 las mujeres | Veo a las mujeres. | Las veo. | I see the women. I see them. |
| 🐕️🐕️ las perras | Veo a las perras. | Las veo. | I see the dogs. I see them. |
| las mesas | Veo las mesas. | Las veo. | I see the tables. I see them. |
| las casas | Veo las casas. | Las veo. | I see the houses. I see them. |

## Direct-Object Minimal Difference

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Veo a los hombres. | Los veo. | I see them. |
| Veo a las mujeres. | Las veo. | I see them. |
| Veo los libros. | Los veo. | I see them. |
| Veo las mesas. | Las veo. | I see them. |

English uses `them` in every sentence.

Spanish distinguishes masculine or mixed groups with `los` and feminine groups with `las`.

# Indirect Object: Les

`Les` represents plural recipients. It does not indicate gender.

| Reference | Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| 👨👨 los hombres | Digo la verdad a los hombres. | Les digo la verdad. | I tell the men the truth. I tell them the truth. |
| 👩👩 las mujeres | Digo la verdad a las mujeres. | Les digo la verdad. | I tell the women the truth. I tell them the truth. |
| 👨👩 mixed group | Doy el libro al hombre y a la mujer. | Les doy el libro. | I give the man and woman the book. I give them the book. |
| 🐕️🐕️ los perros | Doy comida a los perros. | Les doy comida. | I give the dogs food. I give them food. |
| 🤖🤖 los robots | Doy instrucciones a los robots. | Les doy instrucciones. | I give the robots instructions. I give them instructions. |

`Les` can refer to:

- men;
- women;
- mixed groups;
- animals;
- objects or organizations.

Context identifies the recipients.

# Direct and Indirect Minimal Difference

| Grammatical role | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| masculine direct object | Los veo. | I see them. |
| feminine direct object | Las veo. | I see them. |
| indirect object | Les digo la verdad. | I tell them the truth. |
| indirect object | Les doy el libro. | I give them the book. |

Compare:

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Veo a los hombres. | Los veo. | I see them. |
| Veo a las mujeres. | Las veo. | I see them. |
| Digo la verdad a los hombres. | Les digo la verdad. | I tell them the truth. |
| Digo la verdad a las mujeres. | Les digo la verdad. | I tell them the truth. |

# After a Preposition

Spanish uses `ellos` for masculine or mixed groups and `ellas` for feminine groups.

## Para Ellos and Para Ellas

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Hago el café para los hombres. | Lo hago para ellos. | I make the coffee for the men. I make it for them. |
| Hago el café para el hombre y la mujer. | Lo hago para ellos. | I make the coffee for the man and woman. I make it for them. |
| Hago el café para las mujeres. | Lo hago para ellas. | I make the coffee for the women. I make it for them. |

## Con Ellos and Con Ellas

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Hablo con los hombres. | Hablo con ellos. | I speak with the men. I speak with them. |
| Hablo con el hombre y la mujer. | Hablo con ellos. | I speak with the man and woman. I speak with them. |
| Hablo con las mujeres. | Hablo con ellas. | I speak with the women. I speak with them. |

## De Ellos and De Ellas

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Recibo un mensaje de los hombres. | Recibo un mensaje de ellos. | I receive a message from the men. I receive a message from them. |
| Recibo un mensaje de las mujeres. | Recibo un mensaje de ellas. | I receive a message from the women. I receive a message from them. |
| Los libros son de los estudiantes. | Los libros son de ellos. | The books belong to the students. They belong to them. |
| Las casas son de las mujeres. | Las casas son de ellas. | The houses belong to the women. They belong to them. |

## Sobre Ellos and Sobre Ellas

| Full context | Pronoun form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Hablo sobre los hombres. | Hablo sobre ellos. | I speak about the men. I speak about them. |
| Hablo sobre las mujeres. | Hablo sobre ellas. | I speak about the women. I speak about them. |

# Combined Object Pronouns: Se

When `les` appears before `lo`, `la`, `los` or `las`, it changes to `se`.

In these constructions, `se` can mean `to them`.

## Se Lo

| Full context | Combined form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Doy el libro a los hombres. | Se lo doy a ellos. | I give the men the book. I give it to them. |
| Doy el libro a las mujeres. | Se lo doy a ellas. | I give the women the book. I give it to them. |
| Muestro el robot a los estudiantes. | Se lo muestro a ellos. | I show the students the robot. I show it to them. |

## Se La

| Full context | Combined form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Doy la llave a los hombres. | Se la doy a ellos. | I give the men the key. I give it to them. |
| Doy la llave a las mujeres. | Se la doy a ellas. | I give the women the key. I give it to them. |
| Explico la respuesta a los estudiantes. | Se la explico a ellos. | I explain the answer to the students. I explain it to them. |

## Se Los

| Full context | Combined form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Doy los libros a los hombres. | Se los doy a ellos. | I give the men the books. I give them to them. |
| Doy los libros a las mujeres. | Se los doy a ellas. | I give the women the books. I give them to them. |
| Muestro los robots a los estudiantes. | Se los muestro a ellos. | I show the students the robots. I show them to them. |

## Se Las

| Full context | Combined form | English |
|---|---|---|
| Doy las llaves a los hombres. | Se las doy a ellos. | I give the men the keys. I give them to them. |
| Doy las llaves a las mujeres. | Se las doy a ellas. | I give the women the keys. I give them to them. |
| Explico las respuestas a los estudiantes. | Se las explico a ellos. | I explain the answers to the students. I explain them to them. |

The phrases `a ellos` and `a ellas` clarify that `se` means `to them`.

# Them Versus Themselves

English distinguishes `them` from `themselves`.

Spanish distinguishes normal direct objects from reflexive pronouns.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los hombres ven a los niños. Los ven. | The men see the children. They see them. |
| Los hombres se ven en el espejo. | The men see themselves in the mirror. |
| Las mujeres ayudan a los estudiantes. Las ayudan. | The women help the students. They help them. |
| Las mujeres se ayudan. | The women help themselves. |

For normal direct objects:

- `los` represents masculine or mixed `them`;
- `las` represents feminine `them`.

For reflexive actions:

- `se` represents `themselves`.

# Reciprocal Se

`Se` can also mean `each other`.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El hombre y la mujer se ven. | The man and woman see each other. |
| Los amigos se ayudan. | The friends help each other. |
| Las mujeres se escriben. | The women write to each other. |

Context distinguishes `themselves` from `each other`:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los hombres se ven en el espejo. | The men see themselves in the mirror. |
| Los hombres se ven todos los días. | The men see each other every day. |

# **Think About** Something

English **think about/of** normally maps to **pensar en** rather than a literal translation of **about**.

| Spanish | English |

| Pienso en el problema. | I think about the problem. |

# **Think** for an Opinion

When **think** introduces an opinion, Spanish commonly uses either **pensar** or **creer**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Pienso que funcionará. | I think it will work. |
| Creo que funcionará. | I think it will work. |

I think the answer is correct. Use **believe** when emphasizing that you accept something as true: **Creo que su explicación es correcta.**
I believe her explanation is correct.

# **This, That, These**, and **Those**

These determiners show number and relative distance.

| | Near | Far |
|---|---|---|
| singular | this cat | that cat |
| plural | these cats | those cats |

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| este gato / esta gata | this cat |
| ese gato / esa gata | that cat |
| estos gatos / estas gatas | these cats |
| esos gatos / esas gatas | those cats |

English forms do not change for grammatical gender.

Without a noun, the same words are demonstrative pronouns:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Esto es importante. | This is important. |
| Eso es importante. | That is important. |

# **Though** Meaning Despite the Fact

Use **though + complete idea** to introduce a fact that doesn't prevent the main result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque estaba cansada, terminó el informe. | Though she was tired, she finished the report. |

# **Although**

**Although** has the same core meaning as connector **though** and often sounds slightly more formal.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque el apartamento es pequeño, tiene mucha luz. | Although the apartment's small, it's got plenty of natural light. |

Don't use **but** in the same connection: not *Although it's small, but it's bright*.

# Sentence-Final **Though**

Informal sentence-final **though** adds a contrast after the main statement.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El apartamento es pequeño. Sin embargo, tiene mucha luz. | The apartment's small. It's got plenty of natural light, though. |

This placement is common in conversation.

# **Even Though**

**Even though** introduces a real fact and emphasizes the surprising contrast.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque llovió toda la mañana, jugamos el partido. | Even though it rained all morning, we played the game. |

The rain actually happened.

# **Even If**

**Even if** introduces a possible or imagined condition that won't change the result.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Incluso si llueve mañana, jugaremos el partido. | Even if it rains tomorrow, we'll play the game. |

The rain is only a possibility.

# **Even If** Versus **Even Though**

**Even if** is conditional; **even though** presents a fact.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque ya está lloviendo, saldré; incluso si empeora, no cambiaré de plan. | Even though it's already raining, I'll go out; even if it gets worse, I won't change my plans. |

# **But...Not..., Though**

Sentence-final **though** can soften or qualify a negative contrast.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me gusta el diseño, pero no compraría ese color. | I like the design, but I wouldn't buy that color, though. |

In many contexts, choose either **but** or final **though**; using both can sound deliberately conversational.

# **As Though**

**As though** means **as if** and describes how something seems.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Habla como si supiera todo, pero ni siquiera leyó el informe. | He talks as though he knew everything, but he didn't even read the report. |

# Description + **Though**

Formal **description + though + person + verb** means although that description is true.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Por difícil que fuera, no abandonamos el proyecto. | Difficult though it was, we didn't abandon the project. |

This pattern is more literary than **Although it was difficult...**

# **Though** Versus **However**

Both can mark contrast, but **however** often starts a new carefully punctuated statement; **though** can connect or end one.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El plazo era corto; sin embargo, terminamos. Fue estresante. | The deadline was short; however, we finished. It was stressful, though. |

# Informal Spelling **Tho**

**Tho** is a phonetic informal spelling of **though** used in texts and online speech.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue una buena película, aunque un poco larga. | It was a good movie—kinda long, tho. |

Use **though** in standard writing. **Tho** isn't a standard contraction.

# **All the Same**

**All the same** means despite what was just mentioned.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Sé que es tarde, pero de todos modos voy a llamar. | I know it's late, but I'm going to call all the same. |

It overlaps with **even so** and **nevertheless**.

# Pronunciation: **Though, Thought, Through**, and **Tough**

These similar spellings have four different vowels or endings: **though, thought, through, tough**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aunque pensé bien el problema difícil, lo resolví por completo. | Though I thought through the tough problem, I solved it thoroughly. |

**Though** has no common exact homophone; **thoroughly** adds another high-confusion spelling.

# Sentence-Final **Though**

In informal English, **though** can appear at the end of a sentence and mean **sin embargo**, **eso sí** or **aunque**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El apartamento es pequeño. Sin embargo, tiene mucha luz natural. | The apartment is small. It has plenty of natural light, though. |

Sentence-final **though** creates a contrast with the previous statement. For a clear core sentence, use either **but** or final **though**; casual speakers sometimes combine them for extra emphasis.

# Physical Path **Through**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Caminamos por el bosque y atravesamos un túnel. | We walked through the forest and went through a tunnel. |

**Through** presents the area or object as the interior path of movement.

# Opening or Medium

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| La luz entró por la ventana y pude ver a Ana a través del vidrio. | Light came through the window, and I could see Ana through the glass. |

**Through** can identify an opening or the material/medium that something passes across.

# Through a Time Period

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Trabajamos durante toda la noche y terminamos al amanecer. | We worked through the night and finished at dawn. |

**Through** presents activity continuing across an entire period, often despite difficulty or interruption.

# Process or Means: **Through**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Resolvieron el conflicto mediante la negociación. | They resolved the conflict through negotiation. |

**Through** can identify the process, channel, or experience that produces a result.

# **Throughout**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llovió durante todo el día y hubo demoras por toda la ciudad. | It rained throughout the day, and there were delays throughout the city. |

**Throughout** means across every part of a time period or place.

# **Through** Meaning to the End

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Lea el contrato completo antes de firmarlo. | Read the contract through before signing it. |

Here **through** emphasizes continuing from the beginning to completion.

# **Through**: An Inside Path

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Entramos al túnel, lo atravesamos y salimos al otro lado. | We entered the tunnel, went through it, and came out on the other side. |

The core picture of **through** is a path into something, across its interior, and beyond it.

# Movement with **By** and **Through**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Vinimos por el centro, pasamos junto al parque y condujimos por el túnel. | We came through downtown, went by the park, and drove through the tunnel. |

Common movement verbs with either word include **come, go, get, run, walk, drive**, and **take** something or someone.

# **Through** vs **Across**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Caminamos por el bosque y después cruzamos la plaza. | We walked through the forest and then across the square. |

**Through** emphasizes an interior or surrounding space. **Across** emphasizes movement from one side to the other over a surface or area.

# **Through** vs **Throughout**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Caminamos por el edificio y vimos cámaras por todo el edificio. | We walked through the building and saw cameras throughout the building. |

**Through** traces a path or duration. **Throughout** distributes something across every part of a place or period.
